subtopic: DIVIDEND PAYMENTS BY CANADIAN SUBSIDIARIES OF U.S. COMPANIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Is it a fact that wholly owned subsidiaries of United States firms in Canada have increased payment of dividends to their parent companies in the United States, and are thus greatly worsening our balance of payments problem with the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: DIVIDEND PAYMENTS BY CANADIAN SUBSIDIARIES OF U.S. COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume that question was precipitated by a story in the business section of the Globe and Mail this morning, and I anticipated it. The period reported on is prior to the application of the United States direct investment guide lines to Canada, and before the introduction of our own program of guiding principles.
The United States survey covering transactions of United States parents and their Canadian subsidiaries showed a somewhat larger proportion of profits paid out as dividends in 1965 as compared to 1964. However, the rate of dividend payment as reported at 47.6 per cent of the profits in 1965 was not extraordinarily large. On the other hand a substantial volume of financing continued to flow from the United States parents to their Canadian affiliates.
Careful attention is being given to any possible effects of the United States guide lines on Canadian companies and, as I stated previously, any shifts in financing arrangements between Canadian subsidiaries and their United States parents have not prevented the realization in Canada during 1965 and


again in 1966 of substantially larger capital expansion programs. We are, however, keeping this matter under closer review.

maintopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.-REPORTED INTENTION TO CLOSE RADAR LABORATORY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.-REPORTED INTENTION TO CLOSE RADAR LABORATORY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence a question which will not require the assistance of propaganda agents to be answered. My question relates to the Prince Albert radar laboratory, commonly known as "PARL". I received an indication of the intention to close this facility just before coming into the house. Will the minister indicate whether representations will be acceptable to the government from the city council of Prince Albert, the chamber of commerce and scientific bodies to the effect that the work being done by this institution has not been completed? I am wondering whether it is merely coincidental that this particular station is to be closed down at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.-REPORTED INTENTION TO CLOSE RADAR LABORATORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we naturally would welcome representations from any group of individuals, either civic or scientific. I can assure my hon. friend that this station was not scheduled for closing without a great deal of thought. As a matter of fact it was recommended for closing a year ago, but we kept it in operation for an extra year in an effort to determine whether some group in the country such as a university would take over some of the functions previously carried out by the Defence Research Board. If the right hon. gentleman can persuade any group or educational institution in this country to assume responsibility for this station he will receive every co-operation of the Department of National Defence in making the equipment available, and in every other way possible. I believe that would be a good solution, but so far we have not been able to find sufficient 
interest on the part of a responsible organization to make this kind of transition possible.

maintopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.-REPORTED INTENTION TO CLOSE RADAR LABORATORY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the minister indicate whether the University of Saskatchewan, which has a high reputation for scientific research, has been consulted in this connection? Has President Spinks been consulted? He is known to the officials of the Department of National Defence for his outstanding work. Perhaps the minister will also indicate whether the government would continue to pay the 14 officers and technical personnel connected with that station if the University of Saskatchewan were prepared to operate it.

maintopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.-REPORTED INTENTION TO CLOSE RADAR LABORATORY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I suspect that the problem is really financial. I understand there have been consultations with the university. As a matter of fact it is because some of the university students are doing work there this spring that we are keeping it in operation for some additional period. We are doing this in order that they may complete the projects they have under way at the present time. I think if some reasonable method of financing could be worked out at the university level, either there or in co-operation with other universities, we would be glad to receive any submissions they might care to make. But it has been decided by the Defence Research Board that the continued operation by our department is not justified, with respect to the actual need for it at this time.

maintopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.-REPORTED INTENTION TO CLOSE RADAR LABORATORY
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I would ask the minister, are there any more of these radar institutions across Canada? If so, are they being kept open? Also, in view of the fact that the work has to do with the aurora borealis, there must be further scientific research that could take place, as the minister suggested, and does he not think this work might be carried out by the universities?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.-REPORTED INTENTION TO CLOSE RADAR LABORATORY
speechtext: Order. I suggest to the right hon. gentleman and the Minister of National Defence that perhaps we are going a little too far in the consideration of this matter. Perhaps it is urgent, but I do not think we should engage in much more discussion of the subject.

maintopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.-REPORTED INTENTION TO CLOSE RADAR LABORATORY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I simply point out that until I received a notice this morning, as member for that constituency, there was never a word said to me by the minister or the department.

speechtext:
No,
Mr. Speaker, I wish to return to the debate for a particular purpose and reason. First of all I want to thank the minister for his prompt replies to various matters which I brought to his attention with respect to taxation and so on. May I say that the minister, who is so delectable socially, unfortunately considers himself financially impregnable when it comes to the question of budgets.
Before I continue I should like to mention that after having spoken to a number of people in the press gallery I discovered that their feelings were hurt when they were referred to as vultures. I told one member this morning that I would correct that. I believe it is safe to say that the press gallery represents two doves, and the rest of the press are hawks.
Last Monday the hon. member for Kootenay East, who is parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport, delivered an amazing speech both in my view and in the view of the members of this group and of other hon. members in the house. Mr. Speaker, we are studying for the fifth day the mini-budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). The main provisions of that posthumous birth, since the mini-budget came nine months after the main budget of March 1966, boil down to this: starting on January 1, 1967 the maximum personal income tax deduction for old age security is increased from $120 to $240 per year and the sales tax is increased from 11 to 12 per cent.
The income tax increase for old age security applies to one third of the taxpayers with higher incomes, that is 2,300,000 out of 6,500,000.
The sales tax increase will not apply to building materials or to production machinery and equipment. The hike in the sales tax will lead to a price increase, but will not mean more than a one-point boost in the cost of living.
The minister foresees a $340 million deficit for this fiscal year, as compared with one of $150 million forecast by him last March.
The present rate of economic growth is such that expansion can continue without inflation.
Salary and price increases are still excessive, but tend to became moderate.
Those are, sir, the major points that come out of this mini-budget. If the main budget of March 1966 had not made Canadians too enthusiastic, this mini-budget, in turn, deepens the frustration of millions of Canadians. I want to read to the house what Roland Charbonneau, editorial writer at the Sherbrooke Hebdo, has to say about this minibudget, and I quote:
This is further proof that Mr. Lester B. Pearson's Liberal government, and particularly his Minister of Finance, Mr. Mitchell Sharp, are incompetent in the field of public economy.
(Mr. Herridge.l
While increasing old age pensions by 40 per cent, he doubles the contributions of individuals so that the $120 maximum contribution to the Old Age Pension Fund is now set at $240.
Sure, the manufacturers will pay the 1 per cent sales tax increase, but they will collect that, and more, by raising wholesale prices.
And if we follow the sales pattern, once again we find that this additional tax burden falls upon the consumers' shoulders, the majority of whom earn small and modest incomes.
It might be acceptable if the manufacturers and retailers did not go beyond this 1 per cent increase. But experience has shown that whenever the tax is raised on a particular product, the retail price is increased a lot more.
Those are the very sound comments of an editorial writer for the Sherbrooke Hebdo.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, in the eyes of knowledgeable Canadians, this mini-budget certainly did not provide dynamic and progressive measures to solve the various economic and industrial problems of our country.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Just read, for instance, several warnings, and I quote this one given early last January by Mr. R. B. MacPherson, economist with DuPont of Canada:
The Canadian economy is heading toward a period of recession that will reach its peak between the latter half of 1968 and 1970.
In addition, here is the statement of a man who, for several years, has not feared to express himself on Canadian problems, whose judgment has proved sound, far more sound than the measures we are offered by the Minister of Finance in his budgets, since he has taken over that post. I am referring to Mr. A. T. Lambert, president of the Toronto-Dominion Bank.
Dealing with the need for a reasonable stability in prices, Mr. Lambert said the following in mid January 1967:
This is an urgent problem and we cannot remain indifferent in the face of the level of inflation now reached. We cannot ignore either that this factor may have far-reaching consequences for the Canadian economy. Inflation darkens the economic future and if we fail to check it, we are in danger of bringing about a reaction which would have unpleasant effects for all Canadians.
Is it still necessary to emphasize the meaning of the brief submitted to the government a few days ago by the C.L.C.? This responsible, democratic and representative body gives fair and proper warnings to the federal government and to the Minister of Finance and I quote:
The Canadian Labour Congress is concerned that the country may suffer increased unemployment and slip into the slow rate of growth and the high level of unemployment which struck the Canadian economy from 1957 to 1962.


The Canadian Labour Congress report also says:
The rate of increase of the gross national product has diminished substantially. The number of housing starts is considerably lower as compared to 1965, and we have noted remarkable reductions in the sale of some durable consumer goods. Pundits of the business world anticipate a reduction in capital expenditures this year.
And the brief goes on:
-the leaders of this great labour organization are calling on the federal government to refrain from imposing any general restrictive measure, either monetary or fiscal, "that would only accelerate the slackening of the economy'', which seems to have begun already.
People often find exaggerated and too systematic the complaints and grievances presented in this house. I have the privilege to sit here as a free man without any political affiliation and I am here to represent all the electors, men and women, of the Sherbrooke constituency, the great majority of whom, namely about 72 per cent, belong to the class of average Canadian citizens, namely the labour class and office workers of small businesses. Now, the great majority of Canadians are included in that category. My electors, male and female, and millions of Canadians, and also people as well versed in the matter as the hon. Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp), his advisers, his officials, criticize this government and warn it, because the government itself does not seem to know where it. is going. All those people complain that the economic, financial and fiscal philosophy of this government is not distinguishable, no more than its economic direction, at the industrial level and in all the fields of social legislation.
It is a government which gropes along, with inconsistency and which does not prevent problems and events and which awakes only when a complaint has become very severe to apply what is quite quaintly described as a poultice policy. He waits until the abscess or the tumour has become enormous before he treats it or removes it.
That is a backward policy which Canada can well do without in these rather difficult times.
I say the Pearson government is irresponsible and hesitant. It is assertively irresponsible. It refuses to make decisions, or puts them off indefinitely. It intervenes when it is too late and then propounds disjointed and contradictory theories. This want of vigour and courage not only costs Canada millions of 23033-816
The Budget-Mr. Allard dollars but prolongs conflicts, worsens situations, spreads distrust and confusion and alienates Canadians from each other, one region from another and one culture from another.
The Pearson government is a past master at procrastinating; it is the very expression of mediocrity and platitude in Canada. There are thousands of examples, Mr. Speaker. What about its refusal and its hesitation to revise the Canadian constitution, a century old, and to create an official parliamentary committee to consider that matter, giving such a responsibility, not to individuals hidden in officialdom, but to legislators in this parliament who have the responsibility and the duty to guide Canada and all Canadians toward a better and more substantial future.
There is also this contempt on the part of the present central government for the rights and needs of the provinces, its timorous and discriminatory policy with respect to bilingualism and equality of the two cultures. The attitude of the government is that of the ostrich with regard to inflation, price increases, monopolies, the decrease in productivity accompanied by an increasing rate of unemployment. This is also reflected by its bourgeois selfishness in restricting credit, distributing national income in a way which is contrary to democratic principles, aggravating cases and areas of poverty by the implementation of pitiful and mathematical legislation.
One could also criticize the non-interference attitude of the government, waiting until disputes arise before taking action and legislating; added to this, we have a lack of foreign and national defence policy based on principles of simplicity, logic, practicality, efficiency and economy; we have a blind and haphazard commercial and industrial policy, where several of our industries are subject to pressures, oppression and even bankruptcy-and I want to mention, in passing, the difficult situation in which the Canadian textile and shoe industries are now placed-and the government has neglected important sectors of our economy, such as housing for small wage-earners, because even the recent proposals made by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) do not meet the needs of the small wage-earner, the average Canadian, the head of a family.
If this government would add a touch of moral and social philosophy to its legislation, there would be criteria enabling the head of a family to raise and shelter his dependants decently, enjoying a reasonable 5 per cent


The Budget-Mr. Allard rate of interest. But no. In spite of the representations made by a number of hon. members, the government goes on its cold-hearted way and once in a while introduces inadequate measures, which do not meet the real needs of the Canadian head of a family.
There is no moral, human and social philosophy in the elaboration of legislation. Indeed, only administrative concern can be found: uniformity, portability, state control, not to mention a heterogeneous cabinet, without cohesive thinking, evasive, obese, marking time, versatile. No doubt Canada lacks leadership and drive, as well as economic, fiscal, financial, commercial, constitutional and patriotic direction. The government should wake up and the centennial year should make it offer at last some means of action to the citizens of Canada and members of parliament, that is a parliamentary committee on constitutional and fiscal reform.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, in spite of the happy innitiatives taken by the premier of Ontario, Mr. Robarts, and the premier of Quebec. Mr. Daniel Johnson-these two provinces represent almost two thirds of the country's population-who call for a conference on the constitution in order to remodel it in a 1967 context, so that all Canadians might close their ranks, work toward the development of this country with a feeling of brotherhood and stop bickering on discussing misunderstandings and imprecisions of the constitution, the federal government is displaying tremendous irresponsibility.
It should be severely blamed for refusing-and this is the position taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in this house since January 18 last-notwithstanding numerous requests, to the members of the house, to the legislators in this parliament, an opportunity to meet, to trust each other's goodwill and intelligence, in order that we might, in fact, formulate precisely, according to the responsibility we hold from the Canadian people, a renovated Canadian constitution, modernized and amended according to the aspirations of Canadians in 1967.
[DOT] (12:20 p.ra.)
That is proof of the Prime Minister's weakness and faint-heartedness, for he refuses to believe in the good faith expressed not only by hon. members but also by the premiers of the two largest provinces which have more than two thirds of the population of Canada.
We have been needing a constitutional court for a long time but this government

refuses to set one up to settle our problems as is done in other countries. I shall bring this up again when the discussion bears solely on this subject and I urge hon. members to study the operation of the constitutional courts in Switzerland, for instance, or in Western Germany. In so doing, hon. members will realize that such a thing is not impossible since it really exists. Members of the constitutional court of Switzerland are not appointed unilaterally, as are the justices of the Supreme Court of Canada which, as it now stands, is inappropriate to solve our constitutional problems. The constitutional court in Switzerland is made up of representatives of the federal legislature and of representatives the Assembly of the cantons, which is the equivalent of our provincial legislatures. Such things are possible and they have been in existence for a long time, in fact, since the constitutional revision in Switzerland many years ago. Why, then, try to run a country by marking time, by playing blind-man's buff, seeking blindly, without finding it, a solution to our problems, letting the country seek its future right and left, in a perpetual see-saw, when energy and enthusiasm should be shown to finally make Canada the most beautiful country in the world, a dynamic country? We have all the possibilities, but the present government refuses to give us the necessary means to enable all Canadians to work hand in hand to make this a dynamic country, a country of brotherhood.
Why is there so much misunderstanding from Halifax to Vancouver? Why are so many Canadians living on such a vast territory, separated by such distances? It is because our present government refuses us the necessary framework and policies to bring all Canadians together, to start the flow of a geyser of brotherhood, friendship and cooperation which our country needs so much to make a future for itself.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make some comments this afternoon while we are debating the merits of the mini-budget, and I can assure you they will be as relevant to the subject as the last speaker's remarks. Let me make a few observations regarding the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the von Thadden incident to show the amount of double talk that pervades the operations of the organization. In fact it is


present in so much of its activities it should be adopted as its trade mark.
Early in January it was announced that a leader of a small German party had been invited by the C.B.C. to come to Canada and take part in a national network show, of course at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada. A considerable uproar followed this announcement and some well justified complaints were made. In response to the complaints that were made regarding this announcement that von Thadden was to be brought to Canada, the president of the C.B.C. issued a statement. I have in my hand a copy of this statement which was provided by the C.B.C. information services. The statement is dated January 16, and leads off as follows:
The following statement by President Ouimet was released to the Canadian Press in Ottawa; C.B.C. news rooms; and dailies in Toronto after 7:40 p.m. January 14, 1967-
Mr. Ouimet was commenting about the fact that the C.B.C. decided not to bring Mr. von Thadden to Canada because of the opposition which arose following the announcement of the C.B.C. In the last paragraph of Mr. Ouimet's statement we find these very interesting words:
This action does not mean that the corporation will abrogate its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information.
These are noble words, almost fit to be carved on some tombstones, but I will not mention whose. I will repeat them:
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
This action does not mean that the corporation will abrogate its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information.
We have been rising in this House of Commons for the past five years asking for information on how the C.B.C. operates, and always getting the same answers; either that the C.B.C. is in a competitive business and never divulges this kind of information, or that the salaries or payments made to stars on the C.B.C. payroll are never divulged.
For instance, I asked how much money was paid to Mrs. Baskin, whose husband was a private member of the House of Commons, and how much was paid to Mrs. Sauve. The reply was quite interesting. I got the answer as to how much was paid to Mrs. Baskin, in which I had no interest whatsoever, and was told I could not get the answer with regard to Mrs. Sauve because the C.B.C. did not divulge
The Budget-Mr. Cowan that kind of information. Talk about a two way answer on the same subject. This is an example of it.
At the time Mr. Ouimet was making this high sounding statement on behalf of the C.B.C. the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked a question of the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), who answers in this house-I do not like to say she "answers", but she represents the C.B.C. in this house. I will not say she answers for them because the answers are always the same, that it is not in the public interest to divulge anything regarding the C.B.C. On January 16 the hon. member for Prince Albert rose in his place and asked a question of the Secretary of State. Part of her answer can be found on page 11819 of Hansard for that day. It was as follows:
But there is the principle of respecting the right of the Canadian people to know what is current in the world-
That was the answer given by the Secretary of State of the Canadian cabinet regarding the von Thadden episode.
It was at this very moment that a Toronto newspaper came up with the interesting discovery that two stars on the C.B.C. John C. Ricker, M.A., of the Ontario College of Education, and John Tupper Saywell, Ph.D., of York University, Toronto, were the joint authors of a book "Nation and Province." I have photostat copies of pages 58, 59 and 60 of this book in my hand. These gentlemen devote a couple of paragraphs to parliament and the press. I have been in the press business all my life, 40 years with Canadian newspapers and Canadian magazines, and feel I am entitled to speak on behalf of Canadian newspapers and the Canadian press.
I object strongly to the idea put out by these two gentlemen who appear regularly on C.B.C. On page 59 of the book, when commenting on the giving of information about parliament, these men have written that newspapers being in private hands, and private radio stations being in private hands, "they may well be reluctant to print or broadcast news or opinions which could have an adverse effect on advertisers' interests."
On page 60 they talk about the "dangerous tendency toward centralization." These are two comments made by these C.B.C. stars regarding private industry which produces in Canada the newspapers and magazines as we know them today. I would like to ask, what is

February 10, 19S7
The Budget-Mr. Cowan the dangerous tendency toward centralization? We see it going on in all fields of activity. I do not know that it is dangerous. I do not know why Messrs. Say well and Ricker should have the audacity to think that because they want to use the adjective "dangerous" in connection with centralization in the publishing world, it becomes dangerous. It is not ipso facto simply because these two men wish to make a comment of that nature.
Before I proceed to their extolling of the merits and virtues of the C.B.C., in their own eyes, I would like to refer to a very unfair attack that was made on three Canadian press representatives last fall through the medium of a C.B.C. commentator, Knowiton Nash. I have in my hands, provided to me by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's Toronto office, 354 Jarvis Street, under date of October 12, 1966, the text of a broadcast by one Knowiton Nash on the national news, August 11, 1966. In the cource of his remarks Mr. Nash created the impression that anyone who accepts free transportation or hospitality from anyone is their slave, is indebted to the host and will report only in a manner acceptable to the host.
Speaking of these three Canadians-and I will make direct reference to a personal friend of mine although I know two of the gentlemen very well-Mr. Lubor Zink of the Toronto Telegram-Mr. Knowiton Nash, who is paid by the C.B.C., commented about their flying to Saigon and pointed out:
The United States agency says that it does not want to identify the newsmen because it says this might lessen their credibility.
He stated that the action of the United States information office in asking these three men to fly to Southeast Asia was in the best press agency approach. During his comments he remarked that they would, of course, be favourable to the host. If Knowiton Nash is so certain in his opinion that people who accept the hospitality of the bureau of information of the United States will be favourable to that bureau or to the United States, what about the C.B.C. that has flown hither and yon both French crews and English crews in Canadian government planes whenever a minister travels abroad or has anything to do somewhere in Canada? If these newspapermen will be influenced by the hospitality shown to them by hosts such as the information bureau of the United States, what about the C.B.C. commentators who are flown hither and yon with government officials, with the government picking up the check?

I cannot see for one moment how the C.B.C., through Knowiton Nash, can comment in this way with respect to private newspapermen when it is simply a case of the pot calling the kettle black. I cannot see any justification for the attack made by Knowiton Nash on August 11 last. These three men, two of whom are well known to me, are independently minded gentlemen and can be counted on to express their opinions whether or not they were the guests of some would-be host at any time.
To come back to Mr. Saywell and Mr. Ricker, I would point out that after they paid their respects to the operators of private newspapers and raido stations in Canada on pages 59 and 60, after referring to the "dangerous tendency toward centralization" they go on with these choice words on page 60:
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, owned by the government and the people of Canada, does an admirable job in keeping the public informed on events in parliament; being the servant of public rather than private interests, its news is impartial.
I did not know I was going to be speaking on the mini-budget this afternoon, but I wonder how many hon. members heard the marvellously impartial newscast of the C.B.C. last night. Maybe the opposition did not know this. According to the C.B.C. last night and this morning, the four opposition parties ganged up last night to defeat the government by a vote of 87 to 75. That is straight from the C.B.C., which according to Mr. Ricker and Dr. Saywell is keeping the public informed. What kind of reporting is that? I admit that the four opposition parties ganged up in an effort to defeat the government last night, but no responsible, self-respecting newspaperman in Canada wrote such a phrase as "the four opposition parties ganged up to defeat the government last night." When the newspaper reporters' reports are available later today I am certain you will find that they said "the four opposition parties ganged up in an effort to defeat the government."
That is just one episode in the news reporting of the C.B.C.-it can be multiplied a thousand times in the course of a year-which illustrates the inaccuracy of the reporting of the C.B.C. Yet Mr. Ricker and Dr. Saywell said:
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, owned by the government and the people of Canada, does an admirable job in keeping the public informed on events in parliament; being the servant of public rather than private interests, its news is impartial.


Has anyone ever tried to get anything out of this public servant? The answer comes saying that that kind of information is not given, that this is a competitive business and they cannot divulge such information.
Relying on the forthright statement of President Ouimet that this action
-does not mean that the corporation will abrogate its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information.
And relying on the statement made by the Secretary of State which reads as follows:
But there is the principle of respecting the right of the Canadian people to know what is current in the world-
I filed a question with the clerk of the house asking the Secretary of State how much money the C.B.C. had paid Professor Saywell and Professor Ricker year by year during the past five years. I did not wish to indicate thereby that the high opinion of these two men for the C.B.C. was based on the money they had been paid. I just wanted to point out that if Mr. Lubor Zink may be influenced by the fact that he is given a free trip to southeast Asia, it is possible that the high opinion of the C.B.C. held by these two men might be based on the amount of money which has been put into their pockets.
Hon. members at that time did not see the answer that came back from the C.B.C., and I must thank the Secretary of State and her parliamentary secretary for being so kind as to show me the letter. It said, despite the statements of Mr. Ouimet and the Secretary of State, this information had never been given in the past and they do not believe that it should be given at this time. If that is not double talk in its purest and simplest form then I do not know the meaning of double talk.
Hon. members saw and heard the Secretary of State rise in the house the other day and ask me whether I would not withdraw the question because the C.B.C. had not been in the habit of giving this information in the past. She did so in spite of the statement she herself made that there is the principle of respecting the right of the Canadian people to know what is current in the world. I said I would transfer the matter for debate, and hon. members will find at page 39 of today's routine proceedings my motion No. 200. I would have waited to discuss the matter perhaps a couple of months from now after the house leader arranged for it to be brought up when the subject was dead, but having the
The Budget-Mr. Cowan opportunity to speak on the mini-budget today I wish to draw this matter to the attention of the Canadian public so they can see the duplicity and double talk which pervades the operations of the C.B.C., and I have given the house a couple of examples. I certainly would like to know how much money was paid to Messrs. Saywell and Ricker during the past five years, year by year, just so we will know whether their opinions are as pure, unadulterated and free as those of Mr. Zink, Mr. Henderson and the third gentleman who went overseas at the expense of the United States government.
I do not wish to speak at any length on the mini-budget, but I should like to put a question to the Minister of Transport, although I do not expect to receive an answer from him before the vote is taken. Three or four years ago when I was a member of the transportation committee a bill was brought before us to incorporate the Ottawa Terminal Railway Company. One of the clauses in that bill specified that there would be a monopoly operation of the taxicab service at the proposed new Ottawa station. Quite a few of us are incensed at the monopoly operation of taxicab service out of airports throughout Canada stretching from Victoria to St. John's, Newfoundland. This is taking place despite the fact that the cabinet talks about free enterprise and the competitive system, and while they do not allow the setting of prices by competitors. They have a law to prevent collusion by competitors but whenever competition rears its ugly head around an airport or a station it is amazing how quickly the cabinet forgets its dedication to free enterprise and the competitive price system.
When the Ottawa Terminal Railway Company Bill was brought before the committee and objections were raised to the last clause, we were told that it would be struck out. I must give credit to the Minister of Transport for having seen to it that the clause was struck out. We were then presented with a new bill in which the late member for Hull, a highly regarded friend of mine, Alexis Caron-I am sorry he is not with us now -raised an objection to the composition of the board of directors. The bill never did come before the House of Commons. We waited for a new bill with regard to the Ottawa terminal station but it never came forward, and now we are told that the new Ottawa station is being run co-operatively by the C.P.R. and the C.N.R.


The Budget-Mr. Cowan
Recently when coming off the train in the Ottawa station I noticed with interest that there were starters for the Blue Line taxis, of which there were about 20, to take the travellers to their destinations. I should like to ask the Minister of Transport whether we have moved again into the field of a monopoly operation by a taxicab company in the new station. When I spoke to one of the starters on the platform he informed me that that taxicab company had just got the contract. This means that another monopoly is in operation right here in Ottawa under the nose of the cabinet.
I would like to see a little more faithfulness on the part of the cabinet to the doctrine of free enterprise and competition in business, particularly here in Ottawa. I will not go into a discussion of the Malton airport at this time; there may be another occasion for that.
Before I conclude I should like to ask the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who I believe is doing a magnificent job and certainly is giving satisfaction to a large number of newcomers to Canada in Toronto and in the riding of York-Humber, whether he will be introducing a bill before this parliament is prorogued which will make naturalized Canadian citizens the equals of native born Canadians. At the present time a naturalized Canadian citizen can lose his citizenship by one means or another, while this cannot happen to a native born Canadian. We have been promised that amendments would be brought to the immigration bill which would remove this anomaly among Canadians. We have been promised this in four consecutive speeches from the throne.
The opposition pointed out that in 1919 the Liberal party moved a motion with regard to medicare. I looked up that motion, and found it reads that the Liberal party favoured medicare when the nation could afford the cost. The opposition conveniently dropped that last phrase and simply stated that the Liberal party favoured medicare in 1919 and it took us until 1966 to get around to it.
I have sat through four speeches from the throne in which we have been promised amendments to the citizenship and immigration laws so that naturalized Canadian citizens would not be subject to loss of their citizenship for any reason whatsoever. This has never been introduced to the house. I am sure if it were brought forward it would be passed in no time. I cannot imagine anybody in the opposition, and certainly no one on the government side of the house, objecting to

such a bill; yet after being mentioned four times in speeches from the throne it has not yet come forward. Do we have to wait for another 47 years, like the medicare bill, to have this anomaly removed? Can we not let our naturalized Canadian citizens realize right now that they are the equals of native born Canadians once they have gained Canadian citizenship by observing the laws and regulations of this land? As it is now, if certain regulations are broken the citizenship of naturalized Canadians may be taken away from them.
I have had personal experience with this in connection with some Italians who were advised by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration that they had lost their citizenship status. The matter was drawn to the attention of Hon. Guy Favreau, the magnificent former minister of immigration, and was corrected at once. I do not believe this situation should be allowed to continue. Every naturalized Canadian should have the same rights as a native born Canadian, and that includes no loss of citizenship unless it is forsworn.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like very much to take a few minutes of the time of the house this afternoon, at the end of my first year in the House of Commons, to voice some of the frustrations with which I have been surrounded since I was elected to this august chamber. These frustrations, it seems to me, have become magnified by the fact that this is the centennial year in our country's history. These frustrations have been magnified further by the constant dialogue we hear, as Canadians, about a search for our identity, whatever that may be. We hear phrases such as the B and B commission, welfare, the C.B.C., housing crisis, war on poverty, pro-American, antiAmerican, and so on. These phrases seem to stick out, and I believe they are symptomatic of the morass of mediocrity in which we as Canadians find ourselves mired in our search for the good life.
Goodness knows, we have heard that term often enough over the past years. I believe that we as Canadians and as parliamentarians have lost track of who we are and where in fact we are going. After all, what do we mean by "the good life" for every Canadian? Is it perhaps the Christmas present of $30 per month in the form of a guaranteed income supplement referred to so proudly by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) in his minibudget? Perhaps in his heart he feels that $30 per month is the answer to all the - problems of the aged. He pointed out, and I agree with this, that he must raise taxes for some in order to make payments to those in need. I have no quarrel with that.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Am I and other Canadians to believe that we shall have the good life with the addition of 1 per cent to the sales tax on prescription drugs? Imagine that increase being imposed in face of the great amount of evidence presented to the committee of the house meeting at this time to discuss high drug costs? To give us the good life there was no change in exemptions in the mini-budget. As a result some married pensioners must pay back some of their increase. They must obey the rigorous
The Budget-Mr. Brand income tax laws of Canada. Is this the good life for all Canadians? It makes one wonder.
We hear voices from the government side, tinged with pardonable pride, saying that these are prosperous times. Are they prosperous while millions of Canadians struggle under the weight of increasing taxes, prices and debts they must assume to keep themselves and their families alive? Is this the good life? Do we have the good life when we can find $10 million to found a feature film industry but at the same time sit idly by and watch some Canadians suffer kidney failure? From this serious disease many die. They die because we do not have enough artificial kidney machines for dialysis. Here we are in our centennial year and not only do we not have enough machines, not only do we have this basic inconsistency, but we have a jury deciding which victims shall be helped and which shall not be helped by means of the kidney machines. The jury passes the ultimate sentence. Not all patients can have their uremia controlled because there is a lack of funds and equipment. Because of this lack patients see their lives ebb away. Ten million dollars is spent for films but not even $1 million is spent to save a particular group of Canadians. Yet these are prosperous times.
These are the times when treasury bench members can point their ministerial fingers with pride at the number of jobs created by the Canada-United States auto parts agreement. These ministers brush off all statistical arguments showing how many have lost their jobs as a result of the pact. Men and families suffer. After all, it is little comfort to be reminded of those who have lost their jobs as a result of entering into the pact when speaking of the new jobs brought about by the pact.
Is this the good life for all Canadians that we are proud of? Is this the heritage we shall leave our children in the second century of our history? Does the government believe the Canadian people are blind? Does it believe that the bland assurances that all is well with the world will blind the average Canadian to what is around him? The average man can see old age pensioners in substandard rooms in rooming houses, children running ragged in city slums and Indians on our reserves, their pride gone and spirit broken, huddling together in one room. I wonder sometimes whether our Indians are not trying to protect themselves from the white man's benevolence. Is this the good life for all Canadians? Is it enough, I wonder, for


The Budget-Mr. Brand the government to express regret when four or five children on an Indian reserve are burned to death and in the next breath answer a member in the house, as happened the other day, with the words: "What's the matter? Don't you like prosperity?"
Are we expressing Canadianism and the idea of the good life when we find that centennial projects include such things as providing plumbing facilities for prairie towns and putting our fighting men into green gabardine? It may be necessary for some prairie towns to have good plumbing and the amenities of modern life, but do we regard plumbing as a centennial project? Surely the aim of government should be to see that all Canadians have the good life. Instead of spending everything on material things we should spend a little providing something for the mind.
It is time that not only we in the house but people all over Canada began to build a Canadian pride, to forge a true sense of Canadian destiny. It is time we looked to see what is happening in our own country. It is time to stop being blinded by the glow of our smug self-satisfaction and confused by our national dichotomy. If we suffer from selfsatisfaction it is merely a thin veneer hiding our national uncertainty. Somebody said-I forget who-" Let's stop being a nation bounded on the north by the aurora borealis and on the south by an inferiority complex." For the centennial year let us stop being French Canadians, English Canadians, German Canadians or what have you and become truly unhyphenated Canadians.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is time the so-called English speaking parts of Canada recognized the basic fact of life, that the French were in Canada for 225 years before confederation and the British for 108 years. It is time our schools taught proper history. It should not stop in French Canada at the Plains of Abraham in 1759 and begin in English Canada when Wolfe died. It is time we started teaching our children about our country. It is a historic fact that when John Cabot sighted Nova Scotia in 1497 he did nothing to colonize it. But when Cartier sailed up the St. Lawrence in 1534 looking for a passage to the Indies he began the great story of our country. There was the great Champlain who founded Port Royal in 1605 and the settlement of Quebec in 1608. Surely we should try to forget dates such as 1759 and the deaths of two great 
military leaders, the Marquis de Montcalm and General Wolfe.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
I believe that we in this house and certain of the schools across the country have failed in the duty to teach the children exactly what we have here in Canada. I ask my English speaking compatriots to realize that in many ways the French have a greater right to be here than we have. I believe we should recognize this fact and go on from there. I do not believe this is a time for recrimination. It is a time for toleration. It is a time to accept each other as equal partners in this great and glorious Canada of ours.
In my view we should stop wasting our energies and talents on deciding foreign policies for other countries. I believe we should start playing a role as an individual nation. We waste far too much time in this house discussing whether or not the United States is doing the right thing in Viet Nam. I find it difficult at times to put into words how strongly I feel about these things but perhaps as I grope for the right expressions Your Honour will understand the ideas I am attempting to articulate.
I mentioned Viet Nam. I believe we should stop criticizing one or other of the parties concerned and start criticizing ourselves. Regardless of the rights and wrongs of this situation, certain facts are self-evident. One of them is-and I speak as a physician in this sense-that there are men, women and children, non-combatants, in that strife-tom country who are in need of medical care and medical supplies. Instead of blaming one side or the other for what is happening I should like to see the people of Canada, not just the parliament of Canada, doing something about this situation. I know we are doing something now. But is it enough?
I should like, for example, to see the Canadian Medical Association of which I am a member encouraging doctors, surgeons and plastic surgeons to volunteer their services, as I know many of them are willing to do, for one, two or three months at a time in Viet Nam to help repair the broken bodies of the civilian population who are suffering needlessly as a result of this conflict. I am sure that not only would they volunteer their services but that the great pharmaceutical industry of this country would be willing to donate supplies to help civilians in those areas.
We can go beyond Viet Nam to other areas of the world. Help is being given now by such


wonderful organizations as CUSO, MEDICO and so forth. But it is not enough. I believe that if we as Canadians could voluntarily set out to repair the ravages of war we would do more to build a Canadian identity and give ourselves a place of prominence in the councils of the nations than all the emissaries and missions we could send to Hanoi or Saigon.
In our own country, could we not recognize honestly the extent of our housing problems? Could we not seek to ensure that all our citizens have the means to buy their own homes and that our old folks have a decent place in which to live in their declining years? There are so many areas in our own country which urgently need attention; yet we are so busy trying to solve the problems of the world outside our borders that we cannot see what is in front of our eyes. I believe it is time we found our own identity and tried to do something worth while here in Canada. Then we could hold out a helping hand to other areas of the world which need help.
As I think about this problem I think about the plumbing in prairie towns. I think of my children and what they are learning in school about the centenary. Plumbing does not seem to have any heritage associated with it. It does not seem to provide very much by way of a Canadian identity though perhaps it sets us apart from those countries which do not have plumbing. What does it do for Canadians as such?
I believe it is time in our centennial year for us to begin to honour those Canadians who for too long have remained unsung in their native land. Put their pictures on our postage stamps. It is very good to see a puffin or a loon or other wildlife of our country. But how about some of those people who have done so much? How about Pierre Radisson?

speechtext:
I am pleased to hear it. I believe that in every possible way, not only on our stamps but through broadcast and other media, we should put the lives of great Canadians into proper perspective in song and story and allow our children to see that there really are Canadians whose lives and works are just as fascinating as those of Daniel Boone or Jessie James.
I mentioned Pierre Radisson. I might mention another man in whom I am perhaps even more interested because he was essentially a physician. Since the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) is here I would point out that Canadian
The Budget-Mr. Brand physicians have not fared well in having their likenesses placed on postage stamps. I believe that Alexander Graham Bell was so honoured at one time, but his doctor's degree was an honorary one.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Charles Tupper.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Charles Tupper was on a stamp because he was at one time prime minister. It is true he was a doctor. But what about Sir William Osier? What about Robert Tait Mackenzie? Hon. members ask:	Who is
Robert Tait MacKenzie? Many people will not know anything about the life of this great Canadian. Most people will admire what he has done without realizing to whom their admiration is directed. Let me give a brief biographical sketch of this great Canadian. He was born in Almonte, Ontario, on May 26, 1867, 100 years ago, and like so many of the geniuses nurtured in Canada he died an expatriate in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on April 28, 1938. Despite the fact that Dr. MacKenzie spent many of his working years in the United States he remained a Canadian in every way. Every summer throughout his sojourns below the 49th parallel he returned to Almonte to the home he called The Mill of Kintail, named after the ancient seat of the clan MacKenzie.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Why, you may ask, is Robert Tait MacKenzie worthy of centennial recognition?
I see that the Postmaster General wonders too. In 1892 he graduated in medicine from McGill University and, because of his intense interest in physical education, became the first professor in charge of physical education at that institution. His work in the field of physical education became known through many publications and was continued at the University of Pennsylvania and indeed all across the free world. He was in fact one of the prime movers in emphasizing the need for a healthy body to house a healthy and alert mind. A classmate in his early school years by the name of James Naismith, who also became a physician, went on to fame in the United States as the founder of the game of basketball.
While Tait MacKenzie was carrying on his duties as medical director of physical education at McGill University he was also teaching anatomy. He looked for a better method by which to teach anatomy to his students. He had a hobby, that of sculpture, and he decided to put that talent to use in the anatomy


The Budget-Mr. Brand laboratory as a means of teaching his classes. He did sculptures of various parts of the human form in order to illustrate his points. It was not long before these rough clay models were recognized for their intrinsic beauty as well as for their practicality. Following this he enlarged his work to include sculpture of athletic forms considered by many to be the finest of their kind since the days of the classical Greek sculptors.
It is an interesting aside and of great importance to me in Saskatchewan that the figure of the swimmer on the top of the trophy for intercollegiate swimming in western Canada was donated by Robert Tait MacKenzie. This statue has become famous as "The Plunger". If you should see a statue of a swimmer it would likely be a copy of this piece of sculpture. His work and fame as a sculptor grew until finally his sculpture took him literally around the world. Among his works are included the Scottish-American memorial at Edinburgh, the statue of General James Wolfe in London, the "Youthful Benjamin Franklin" at the University of Pennsylvania, and many, many more. Members of this house who are not familiar with his work may see the statue of Captain Guy Grum-mond in the archives in this city and, in the foyer outside this chamber, the heroic statue of Lieutenant Colonel George Harold Baker, M.P., executed by Robert Tait MacKenzie.
Despite what this man did in his lifetime there is no argument that he did not receive the honour due him by his countrymen. It seems only fitting that this authentic genius of Canadian birth who had great pride in Canada should on the centennial of his birth and in the centennial year of our history receive from his countrymen the honour that was denied him during his lifetime. What this honour should be I leave to the Secretary of State and to the centennial commission. I am sure the minister, in co-operation with the Canadian Medical Association and the council on health, physical education and rehabilitation, can come up with a fitting memorial for this great genius. His sculpture has been given to the world. His fellow countrymen should recognize its origin.
To my French speaking friends let me say that Robert Tait MacKenzie believed very much in the importance of French culture within our nation. One of his first accomplishments was to become proficient in the French language, so much so that at one time in his career he was invited to France by the government of France, which of all the European

continental countries appealed to him most. As a result of this invitation he helped to put in practice in France a system of rehabilitation which assisted in restoring the manpower of that country after the devastating losses of the first world war.
His home, The Mill of Kintail, still stands. Many members here may have seen it. Many of his original works still decorate the studio. This is due not to government help but to the interest of the present owner of the mill, Colonel James F. Leys. I should like to see something done in our centennial year to honour this man.
There are many other Canadians who fall in the same category and perhaps could become household words so that when the children come home from school they will say, "Did you hear about so and so? We learned about him in school today." I think we must do these things now in our centennial year. We should do something within our country to build a true Canadianism-one country, one Canada, with all citizens having equal rights. We should do something to honour those who in the past have helped make Canada the great nation it is today.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this is an important debate, dealing as it generally does with a variety of important subjects and with discussion of a general nature. I think it underscores a fact which never should be forgotten, that parliament is something more than a mere legislative mill which eventually turns out the emissions of a government in legislative form. This chamber is a body which seeks and must seek the views, and give thought to the concerns, anxieties and needs, of the people who send us here. Before we bad responsible government we had representative government. I think that in our general debates we emphasize the representative aspects of our democratic structure.
As usual in debates of this kind, and as usual with regard to most constructive utterances in this chamber, the speeches which have been made in this debate have been given little attention in the press with its proclivity for the controversial and sensational and its seeming indifference to the reasoned and the reasonable. Yet in my opinion the remarks by members in the various parts of the house during the past few days have been valuable contributions to important public issues. I say that about many of the speeches I have heard and have read, and I certainly say it about the one just delivered


by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand).
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
When one intervenes in a debate at this stage there always is the difficulty that so many things which one would like to say himself have already been said. I can only express my agreement with many of the contributions which have been made. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) and the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), especially the former, spoke about the procedures of this house. Their comments were thoughtful and I think useful. We must be concerned about the efficiency of our procedures. Smoothness of the operation of this body is not the be-all or end-all-far from it. I would rather we remained hopelessly archaic than that we whittle away or diminish one bit of our freedom of expression. But we do not ensure democratic values by enshrining inefficiency. I think the hon. member for Royal was very helpful to all of us in outlining some important and valuable projected improvements in our procedure. I shall only mention two aspects of this field which are elementary and elemental.
By now we should realize that sessions of parliament are year-round operations. We find now that it is 13 months since we began this session. In other words, the calendar year is not long enough for the parliamentary year. Surely we must recognize that this is a year-round business and schedule our adjournments for appropriate preconsidered times so that they are not subject to constant hit or miss, hope and happenstance, with the result that we never know when we might or might not end a certain session.
I also believe, and this is becoming an old chestnut with me, that we have to look at our voting procedures. During the last vote I attended in this house not long ago-I do not miss very many-I sat for 49 minutes while the bell rang and rang and rang. I do not mind being up so late at night or hearing bells ringing in my ears, but even I could find more useful things to do than sit and wait while bells ring. In this case, after 49 minutes of waiting, I stood up and announced that I was paired with an hon. member who had missed the bell-ringing session. I think we could entrust our democratic procedures to an electronic voting device. We could wait five minutes for the vote to be taken and then cast our votes in five seconds.
Someone told me after the last suggestion I made along these lines that I was doing some

The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie personal pleading. At one time I was accused of being embarrassed and red in the face
because I voted with the New Dtmocratic Party. Let me defend myself and recall that I suggested this procedure long before the time the New Democratic Party was so abundantly right that I voted with them.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), spoke about constitutional developments or the lack of them. I have been disturbed in recent months after the former premier of Quebec torpedoed the Fulton-Favreau formula despite his earlier commitment to it and despite approval by all other legislatures. In the past we have looked for initiative from the national government and the national parliament. I am proud that recently Premier Robarts of Ontario has taken an initiative, but I regret that it was necessary for a leader in the provincial arena to give the lead in matters where the initiative lies with the national parliament, with the national government and with national leaders. But in the vacuum which he as an intelligent Canadian saw, he took an initiative which I heartily welcome.
We should have set up a constitutional committee long ago and we should have invited the legislatures to do something similar. We have great and important problems of a constitutional nature and we should not have sat inert and relaxed during the months which followed the demise of the Fulton-Favreau formula. I salute Premier Robarts in this connection. He has shown himself as a great Canadian. I believe Canada can rejoice in the fact that during the last few years the populous and prosperous province of Ontario has not been led by a Mowat or a Hepburn. Had that been the case the frail fabric of federation might have been badly sagging by this time.
It is now 13 months since this session began and I have been distressed by the paucity of discussion on external affairs. I am convinced that there is a strong desire on the part of the great majority of members in this house to give the widest possible degree of support to the execution of our nation's foreign policy. Irrespective of the label which is borne by the party in power, I believe there is a genuine feeling, which has been in existence for a long time, that our foreign policy should be bipartisan, multipartisan or possibly non-partisan in so far as it is practically possible.
I am convinced that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), sometimes described as a "former political person",


The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie agrees with the virtues and values of departi-sanizing our foreign policy. In this assumption, because I believe him to be a sincere and able internationalist, I offer him a suggestion or two which are intended only to be helpful. I regret that he is not here. When he is not here I do not vote, but I have not taken that self-denying ordinance in so far as talking is concerned.
In the first place, although his practised skill in evasive equivocation is always appreciated as an art form, and it truly is, it is not always universally beneficial to a broadening of the base of parliamentary and public support of his government's actions on the international scene. The broadening of such support should be a goal toward which he should strive. In a word I would say that he should be more forthcoming in his answers to those members who seek information on the many vital areas of Canada's external affairs policy. There is no one in this house, I am sure, who would hesitate for a moment to take on the mantle of silence if he believed that silence, per se, would be conducive to any worth-while accomplishment in our diplomacy. Sometimes I fear that my good and long-time friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, shows an increasing tendency to invoke the aura of high confidentiality around foreign policy areas and incidents which at some times are widely discussed outside this chamber.
How often are we enjoined here in this house to maintain silence on the Viet Nam question lest some imminent solution or impending accomplishment be destroyed utterly by the slightest reference to it in this parliament? We are made fearful lest a phrase, sentence or syllable might mar some impending achievement. Yet Mr. Ronning speaks publicly. How often have we been enjoined to silence in this chamber when later during the same day we have turned on our television sets and heard senators of the United States evoke from the secretary of state, Mr. Rusk, fulsome answers, or indulge in the quizzing of Mr. McNamara, or the eliciting and publicizing of views of a very distinguished newspaperman, Harrison Salisbury? If in the United States, where great responsibility for world affairs resides, their democracy may be so functional as to allow, and indeed encourage, full discussion of vital areas of diplomacy, surely we here, whose responsibility is less, need not be inhibited from exploring and discussing our role in this issue, which of course concerns us although naturally it does not concern us primarily.

[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I think that candour and earnestness in the discussion would be valuable. I believe that the external affairs committee should be much more active than it is. I think we should be examining in depth various aspects of our country's foreign policy and drawing upon the expertise of specialists in world affairs. I am happy that committees generally have become more active and more useful on the parliamentary scene, although I think we have to use a little bit of skill in organizing their schedules. There seems to be something wrong when for many, many weeks no committees are sitting, and then we have a great splurge when there are more committees sitting than members to go around or rooms in which to hold them. But I see an increasing initiative within and on the part of committees, and I think this is to be welcomed. I do not think the external affairs committee should content itself with merely examining the estimates of the department. I think we should move into great questions and help to further our own knowledge and give leadership to our people.
In the far off days of Mackenzie King and O. D. Skelton foreign policy was regarded as something so esoteric as to not really to be suited to the amateurs, members of parliament, let alone the public. Such an attitude was deplorable then but at that time our role in the world was not so important as to make our diplomatic efforts of much significance. It really did not matter too much whether Mr. Skelton and Mackenzie King handled it all themselves or whether there was the odd reference to it in parliament. But things are different now. Canada has a different role and there is a relationship between public opinion and foreign policy. The public, which always had a stake in the decisions of the diplomats, now has far greater influence on the decisionmaking than ever before. Canada is not a great power; we do not have great power roles; we do not have big power responsibilities. But we are capable of making an impact upon the world.
I think we must do all we can to strengthen our role, to make more valuable our contribution. I think that we as parliamentarians could enrich our knowledge and increase our participation in discussions which will lead to the most meaningful policies. We talk often about the various stages in our foreign policy development, how we began in the early days of nationhood with no policy, how people like


Borden led us into an era of responsibility on the world scene, how we carried on in an isolationist attitude in the League of Nations and did nothing while talking about American isolationism at the same time.
In the post-war era, under Mr. St. Laurent we took a positive and valuable role. Perhaps we are now at a stage where we should do something more fundamental in re-examining the situation. I am always a little ill at ease when I hear people say, "Isn't it wonderful that we are so much more popular than the Americans, and that no one dislikes us?" I think possibly we are at a stage of our development when we may have to risk being disliked somewhere in the world as we try to give meaning to the things that we believe are important in world affairs.
I would like to see us take part in a thorough analysis of our role in NATO. What about NATO itself? The dry words of the treaty of 1949 are not of themselves sufficient. What changes should the alliance undertake? What changes does Canada envisage for the alliance and for its own role therein? I wish the minister were here, because he and I used to be companions of the order which supported Canadian membership in the Organization of American States. I have kept my membership in that group intact but I do not think the minister belongs to the club any more. I would like to know why. I was hoping I would be able to salute and applaud him as he led our country into a greater role of hemispheric responsibility. Has he forsaken his belief in Canadian membership, or is it yet to come?
I wonder, too, whether we are taking sufficiently careful note of what is taking place in the United Nations. Is the United Nations itself abandoning what used to be regarded by us as its most hopeful field of operation, namely, the peace-keeping role. Things which have happened in the general assembly of the United Nations cause me grave disquiet. Are we adopting our foreign policy vis-a-vis the United Nations to an attitude which that body has itself abandoned? I am concerned about that.
There are many areas of possible Canadian initiative. What is the status today of the one China, one Taiwan policy? It is an interesting question. Have we yet been able to find a meaningful measure to register in a practical way Canadian disapproval and distaste for the actions of the Ian Smith regime in Rhodesia? Unless that which we are doing on
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie the international scene or in the Commonwealth context has some meaning when applied to the object of the action, it is useless. We should either look for something meaningful or advise our Canadian people that no meaningful role has been found.
Should we be more specific in our external aid programs? Are we spreading our own resources too thin? Should we, for instance, undertake a special role for the small islands in the West Indies to the solution of whose economic and political problems we could make a meaningful and perhaps decisive contribution? I am convinced that there is no part of the world whose future both economically and politically depends more upon Canada than those small islands to the south. I think we should launch into a program that is imaginative, that is new, that is massive. A step has been taken, and we welcome it. But those islands are much more than places for fun in the sun; they are places which will have great difficulty in surviving. This might give us a great opportunity to make the Commonwealth idea mean something more than a mere good will expression in an afterdinner speech. I should like to see us face up to the ultimate responsibility for the small islands in the Caribbean and offer them every economic and political aid that they will accept.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
There are many other problems which I think are ripe for discussion and which the people of Canada would like us to discuss. Some of us believe that Canada would improve its effectiveness on the diplomatic scene by developing full diplomatic relations with the Vatican State, and perhaps it is best that someone from the reformed religious tradition give utterance to that view and underscore the fact that the Vatican State is much more than the seat of a great religious leader. It is a political entity, it is a state among the other states of the world, and I think we could enrich our role greatly and enhance our effectiveness by developing diplomatic ties of a closer nature than we have at present.
There are a host of questions calling for serious appraisal and sustained discussion. I think we limit our effectiveness in the world if we fail to ask questions and seek solutions. I see an item on the order paper relating to the external affairs committee. I agree with my colleague that it is not necessary for the committee to be set up or put in operation by the minister or the Prime Minister. I believe


The Budget-Mr. Kennedy that with greater effectiveness, greater research and a more searching inquiry as to our goals we will bring external affairs out of the area of casual reference and equivocation. I believe we can move toward greater leadership for our country in the world and within this country by those of us who are on the national political scene. I would invite the minister, who is a good minister, to be more fulsome, more frank in his discussions with us.
