subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to make a few comments in this debate which I feel was not necessary because I do not think a mini-budget between regular budgets is necessary for the simple reason that it comes on the eve of the annual budget. Under the arrangements made with regard to the old age pension supplement the payments will not go out at least until the time the next budget is due. Furthermore, there is an accumulation of funds in the old age security account which would
[Mr. Macquarrie.)
allow the payments to be made until such time as the annual budget is brought down.
What concerns me most is that this budget has directed the attention of the taxpayers of Canada to the fact that its purpose is to support the old people of this country. I think this is grossly unfair. If the government is going to single out certain people to budget for especially and to whom special attention must be paid, then I believe the government should go further and do the same in other areas. It should bring down special budgets to cover the costs of expensive royal commissions to which the attention of the public is not drawn too often. For example, the current commission on bilingualism and biculturalism has cost this country now well over $10 million and there seems to be no end in sight. Editorial comments have referred to it as a most expensive exercise in futility.
I am concerned about what has been taking place in recent times with regard to financial matters which has undermined people's faith in investing in their own country. We hear from the government benches diverse opinions on whether we should allow foreign capital into this country or limit ourselves to our own capital. I think that we need both, but we must put most of our efforts into encouraging our own people to invest in our own country.
The public debt of Canada is reputed at the present time to be in the neighbourhood of $1,000 for each man, woman and child. In many funeral services we are told that we bring nothing into this world and we certainly take nothing out of it, but apparently every child who comes into this world in Canada brings with him less than nothing and when he departs leaves less than nothing behind. Not only do we have an inheritance of debt but we are committed to the servicing of this debt which is getting more costly as interest rates go up. At the present time everyone is faced with a charge of $60 to $70 per year to service the debt which we inherited, and the government has made no effort to reduce it. On the contrary, even now in these good times we still face deficits.
A good example of the situation would be a person who inherits a growing farm and instead of paying his way keeps spending money and borrowing money against the property until eventually he has nothing left. Government expenditures in general are directed to consumable goods and services and they are made for things which are useful today but which in future days will either
February 10, 1967	COMMONS
wear out or become obsolete and have to be replaced. I think every encouragement should be given to the government to put more investment into permanent structures, something that will stand for years, such as transportation facilities and other facilities which affect the economy of a particular area.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The recent failures of financial institutions in this country have upset a lot of people. I feel that in this regard the government must move strongly in order to ensure that people who invest in what is known as the trust class of securities will have protection. There is nothing more humiliating for a person than to invest his hard earned savings and find later that the investment is worthless. I say the government should take the lead in this situation because recently there have been indications the government has not even considered honouring some of the commitments of the past. I am referring to the issue in 1936 of $55 million of 3 per cent perpetual bonds. Whether or not the people who purchased them realized they might never be honoured,
I believe that as time went on people treated them as being worth their face value. Since interest rates have risen they have found that these bonds are not tradeable at face value. In other words, these people are stuck with something for which they paid $100 in 1936 only to find that in 1966 and 1967 these bonds will not bring any more than $50 on the market. If you multiply that loss by the amount of inflation which has taken place, you find that the value of these bonds is down to about $20 or $25 on an original investment of $100.
I believe this is a great injustice and should be rectified. If the minister cannot make a new issue at the present time and refund the face value of these bonds, I feel he should set a date a few years hence when these bonds will mature. This action would stabilize the market for the bonds and if people wanted to hang on long enough they would realize their face value. I believe they are entitled to some encouragement to hope that some day they will get the face value of these bonds purchased with money they had put aside in those days.
I believe that the government must provide more funds to aid the country. There should be greater government participation in education in order to assist those who are able to absorb higher education. On the other hand, those who for one reason or another are not able to pursue higher education should also
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy be looked after and something should be done for them. Although some provision is being made now for these people, I think more could be done to bring them to a place where they could participate in the production of the country and earn a decent living for themselves and their families. In this regard the government could also help in the general development of the country in order to provide opportunities for these educated people. There are many parts of this country still underdeveloped. I did say that if Canadians perhaps put more of their money into development through private enterprise, this would provide opportunities for young people. However, private enterprise must be assisted by government in the fields of communication within the country and in trade relations with other countries.
I should like to turn now to a more local aspect of my theme. In the province of Nova Scotia from which I come there is probably more room for development with the limited resources we have than anywhere else in the country. We have an organization called the Atlantic Development Board. It was set up to deal with certain aspects of development in that area. The Atlantic Development Board is very much concerned now with studying the development of tourist attractions in the maritime provinces. In this day and age when highways are better and people have more leisure, the tourist industry is becoming one of our greatest industries.
The Atlantic provinces have much to offer to tourists. We do need more access roads to some of the assets we have there. A highway has been projected from the United States border around the head of the Bay of Fundy to the southwest tip of Nova Scotia. This highway would go through a great scenic area. As a matter of fact, much of the highway is already there but there are certain links that need to be developed in order to make it truly a vacation trail. One of these links is the crossing of a major obstacle near Truro known as the Shubenacadie River. The construction of such a crossing would shorten the mileage and also attract people to the seashore along which are the highest tides in the world as well as many other attractions which one cannot see anywhere else.
This crossing would not only be of great benefit to the tourist industry but also to the people in this area who are in reasonably close proximity, as the crow flys, to the town of Truro which is fast becoming an educational and industrial centre as well as a


The Budget-Mr. Mather health centre as a result of recently expanded facilities. It is only fair to the people in this area that they have access to this town, and a crossing of this major obstacle would reduce the mileage one would have to travel. As a matter of fact, in so far as health is concerned it would probably save lives because of the ability to get medical help quickly.
This trail, I believe, would also benefit another depressed part of that area, namely, the area to the west of Truro which has unfortunately been more or less bypassed by the development of the trans-Canada highway. It is an area which certainly needs some development. Actually it is one of the most beautiful parts of the province. Every effort should be made to get tourists into that area so that they could feast their eyes on the beautiful landscape. I would commend to anyone visiting Nova Scotia the north shore of Nova Scotia and the hundreds of miles of ocean beach which are practically unoccupied and readily accessible along the sunrise trail. Facilities are available there, land is reasonable and the municipalities will co-operate in making it economically feasible for people to move in and build cottages. The waters are warm, sheltered and shallow, suitable for swimnrng in the summer months and good for other water sports. I commend this area to anybody visiting Nova Scotia. They will enjoy it.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

Yes, Brule beach is one place. I have mentioned the high tides in the bay of Fundy. I am glad to know that a study is being made to harness these tides to produce hydroelectric energy. It is estimated, according to experts, that the tides in and around Minas basin alone can develop enough power to heat and light half of North America. It would cost a lot of money to develop this undertaking but once developed it would operate with little cost for 100 years. The government would have to participate in the study until it can be shown to private interests that it would be profitable for them to take over and develop the project. The project would serve generations to come. It is not something which would have to be renewed twice in every generation.
It has been a pleasure to take part briefly in this debate and I thank the house for its attention.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has said: "Well, we have increased the old age pension to certain old age pensioners and now we must find the money to pay for that increase." The only way to do that, he suggests, is by increasing taxes. I hope to contradict his proposition.
To show the mixed-up society we live in and the inflationary spiral in which we are involved, let me point out that before those old age pensioners most in need have received the increase their rents have gone up. We are receiving letters from old people saying their rents have been increased. This situation results from the housing shortage and not from mean landlords. The housing shortage is part of the general inflationary situation. The housing shortage means a greater pressure on rents. Rents are rising not only for young wage earners who may be able to afford them but for old people who have little to exist on. I do not blame the government for the housing shortage, though had it acted earlier and more resolutely the housing situation in Canada could have been better than it is today.
It is only fair to say that though the government might have done better the greatest factor influencing inflation in this country is generated not here but south of the international border. The United States is at war. This is the big fact in North America today. What happens in the United States affects our budget, education, pensions and production. The fact is like it or not, that the United States is at war. We are geared to a warfare state. At this time the United States is spending $55 million a day in Viet Nam, $1 billion a week for general defence purposes and $40 billion a year in general war contracts. This is


a massive injection of public money, representing an increase of debt, into the private enterprise or capitalistic system. In large measure this enormous amount of money is going into the production of non-consumer goods. One result is that there are fewer consumer goods to be bought by the greatly extended numbers of dollars in circulation.
To increase taxes in our country, particularly sales taxes, in the light of the tremendous economic influence and impact we face from the United States will defeat the purposes the minister has set forth. The minister believes that his policy is anti-inflationary. I contend, particularly in regard to the increase in the sales tax, that his policy will lead to higher prices and higher wages followed by even higher prices and higher wages, with the latter pursuing the former.
There is an alternative to increased taxes open to the government. I have been amused, as a former newspaperman, to read the editorial pages of many Canadian newspapers whose editors sagely nod their heads, agreeing with the Minister of Finance that the only way to get money for the increased old age pensions is to increase taxes. Surely there is a simple and clear alternative to increase taxes-reduced spending.
We should be like a family living on a budget. When a family decides to spend more money on one project it decides to spend less money on another. In my opinion we have a great, shadowy area, national defence, where we might well explore a reduction of expenditure. Let me quote figures for the record. In the last 20 years we have spent in the order of $25 billion on defence. We are now spending $1.5 billion yearly. In this country of 20 million people we spend no less than $4.24 million a day on defence. The total federal personal income tax for the fiscal year April 1, 1965, to March 31, 1966, was little more than $2 billion. In that same period we spent more than $1.5 billion on so-called defence. We spent a sum on defence approximately equal to three fourths of all federal personal income taxes. If we also include the hundreds of millions of dollars we spend on veterans affairs and veterans pensions, which are an adjunct of defence, we see that our total defence spending equals practically all the money received from personal income taxes. We have spent $25 billion in the last 20 years on defence. Though we have done this, and I do not think that all the money has been wasted by any means, I have yet to meet
The Budget-Mr. Southam anyone who really contends that in this atomic age Canada can defend herself against nuclear attack. I believe this is an area which ought to be considered seriously before attempts are made to raise more money by increased taxes.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I should like to remind the house of the remarks made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) who spoke on the subject of defence some time ago outlining some of the economies which must be made and suggesting that in line with the realities of 1967 we should change our defence commitments in such a way as to bring about the withdrawal of our brigade and air divisions from Europe, the closing down of the obsolete Bomarc SAGE air defences, and a review of our present antisubmarine role. He went on to say that in place of today's expenditures we should concentrate on a tri-service or unified, efficient force available for peace keeping roles.
I wish to place before the house the general proposition that instead of moving toward increased taxes we should study means of reducing our expenditures. With this point in mind, I intend to vote against the budget resolutions if I have the opportunity to do so.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to take part in the debate on the mini-budget but since I did not have an opportunity to discuss the main budget last year I felt I had a few remarks I would like to make which would be pertinent at this time. Many of the problems which face us have, of course, already been discussed at length by earlier speakers.
I was impressed by the suggestion of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand) that we should mark our centenary by commemorating our great Canadians by portraying them on stamps or by using other means of keeping them before the public eye for a century to come or for several centuries in Canada's future.
When dealing with budgets we naturally think of taxation. That is the first thing which comes to mind. In the past year there has been no lack of evidence as to how unpopular the government is becoming by trying to go too far too fast so far as taxation is concerned. Simple and direct evidence of this can be found in the postponement of the medicare program which had to be sidetracked and put off for a year until July 1, 1968.


The Budget-Mr. Southam
The federal government has increased revenue from income tax and sales tax by about $300 million and will likely raise this sum to $500 million when the national health insurance plan comes into effect. This, of course, is one of the main causes for the rise in the cost of living in Canada until it has reached its highest point in Canadian history. The increase in the present year alone amounted to between 3 and 4 per cent. We are hoping, of course, that the government will take account of some of the suggestions which members of the opposition have put forward during the present debate and on previous occasions to bring about a halt in this inflationary spiral before our goods are priced right out of the world market upon which Canada depends so greatly for its economic survival. All these questions have been discussed already at some length but I refer to them in passing so as to re-emphasize the need to take a serious look at the direction in which we are heading in this centennial year.
I wish to turn now to a subject about which I have been concerned for a long while-our national parks policy. Over the years as a member of this house I have been advocating the development of further parks as well as the development of the tourist industry generally in Canada as one of the basic ways by which we could enhance and accelerate our economy. As we know, Canada is a veritable gem, one of the most beautiful countries in the world. In the last few years I have had the privilege of visiting many parts of the earth's surface and I have come home more satisfied than ever to be a Canadian, to look at this fine land of ours and realize what a potential it has.
If we study our economy we find that our first source of income is the pulp and paper and wood products industry and the second is the export of our agricultural products. Our third source of income-this is not realized by many Canadians-is the tourist industry. Figures indicate that in 1966 the revenue derived from tourism amounted to more than $600 million. In the present year, with the impetus given by the world fair in Montreal, it is anticipated that this figure will reach $1 billion. This shows the extent to which the tourist industry has become an important part of our economy, something to which we should continue to pay serious attention.
I have been advocating a reconsideration of our national parks policy particularly as it applies to Saskatchewan. I was very pleased when the Minister of Indian Affairs and
Northern Development (Mr. Laing) told us a year ago last April that at long last it would be government policy to develop a second national park in the province of Saskatchewan. This statement naturally interested and excited the people of our province. As hon. members know, over the years we have lacked a varied basis for our economy. We have been dependent for the most part on agriculture though in the last 10 or 20 years we have begun to come into our own, thanks to attention from the government, particularly the attention paid to some of our problems by the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). Having come from that province and lived there for many years the right hon. gentleman realized that we could not live by bread alone and began to develop a policy to help the western provinces and, of course, the maritimes, whose problems are somewhat similar to ours in the west. The roads to resources program was a basic part of this policy and it is paying off, as Canadians fully realize.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
As I say, I was glad to hear the minister announce two years ago that we were going to have a second national park. Since then we have been waiting patiently for its finalization. You, Mr. Speaker, will remember that I questioned the minister about it in the house and on one occasion at your discretion I was ruled out of order. I then placed questions on the order paper as to why the new park was not being brought into being. So far nothing definite has been stated about when the park will be developed or where it will be situated in Saskatchewan. Again I point out to the minister that the people of Saskatchewan would like to hear soon when this development will take place. I am disappointed that it is not being developed this year as another centennial project in the economic life of this great land of ours.
A number of years ago, during the time when the party of which I am a member was in office, we discussed diversification of our economy and the desirability of having subsidiary industries located in various parts of the country which lacked industry. We in Saskatchewan felt it was a province in which there should be such diversification. Through automation our agricultural industry was beginning to increase in productivity, but our population loss was becoming very serious because we were not able to provide sufficient jobs for all the young Saskatchewanites we

February 10, 1967	COMMONS
were raising and educating. The young people had to leave home and move to other provinces. Our loss was the other provinces' gain. Bearing in mind the economics of human resources and the potential of having a lot of people in one particular area, I do not need to emphasize how serious was the problem to Saskatchewan.
Of course we had another problem in Saskatchewan for a number of years. The political climate there was not compatible to the retention or development of industry. The C.C.F. party there does not like to be reminded about this, but its policies were such that industry did not feel too happy about the prospects of going into Saskatchewan.
I can think of one example to emphasize this point, Mr. Speaker, where the former government of Saskatchewan took it upon itself to tax oil companies on the road allowances adjoining land which had been leased to them. This irritated some of the companies to such a considerable extent that they deliberately moved their head offices from Saskatchewan to other provinces rather than pay that unfair tax.
Many other such instances could be cited, but it so happens that we now have another free enterprise government in the province. Of course I do not think it will do quite as well as if a Conservative government were in charge of the province, because I do not feel it is doing a better job than we could in inducing industry to establish in Saskatchewan.
One of the things we greatly hoped for in Saskatchewan was the promised heavy water plant which was discussed on numerous occasions in this house. The fact that it did not materialize was a great disappointment to me as the member representing the area in which it was to be developed. It was a great disappointment to Saskatchewan as a whole, and I know it was very embarrassing to the present premier of Saskatchewan when the proposed project fell through.
To me it is passing strange that two years ago the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) announced that tenders had been advertised for a second heavy water plant. He said that the tenders would be considered in January, 1965. In the month of February, 1965, tenders were opened and the minister got up in the house and made a very positive announcement to the effect that the world's largest heavy water plant would be constructed at Estevan, Saskatchewan, with construction to commence about August of that year.
The Budget-Mr. Southam
I do not think I need to relate in great detail the gruesome disappointment that faced the people of Estevan and that part of the province, and the Premier of Saskatchewan, when early in August, 1965, word came over the wires that Western Deuterium Limited had withdrawn its proposal. It had not broken a contract but simply withdrew its proposal to build the plant. Immediately we knew that there had not been any hard and fast agreement with Western Deuterium. The government had just taken the proposal and the minister came into this house and made a positive announcement leading Canadians, particularly the people of Saskatchewan, to believe that at last Saskatchewan was being recognized so far as industrial redistribution was concerned.
I need hardly mention also the furore which was created in the city of Estevan. This was to have been a $40 million plant. You, Mr. Speaker, can appreciate the planning that had to be undertaken in a city like Estevan, with a population of around 9,000 people, to provide the facilities that would be necessary. Such facilities normally cannot be provided overnight. Real estate began to change hands. Several contractors were starting to build apartments to house the 500 people required to build the plant and were making plans to build permanent homes for approximately 200 engineers and technical workers who would be running the plant when it came into operation. The city fathers had to call on the provincial government for support and advice with respect to municipal services that would have to be provided, water facilities, hydro, and sewage. A great deal of expense went into this preparation and it was a very great disappointment to the people of Saskatchewan and the people of this area in particular when the proposal was withdrawn.
Examining the matter in retrospect it seems to me that at that particular time the ministers responsible for national parks policy and the proposed heavy water plant must have been taking advantage of a situation in which they thought they could develop good political propaganda, because everybody seemed to anticipate that there would be an election either in the spring or fall of 1965. These great promises, headlined in the Saskatchewan daily newspapers and supported by the Premier of Saskatchewan himself, made it look as though the federal Liberal government was on its toes and would finally do something for our great province. I maintain that the government now owes us something


The Budget-Mr. Southam to compensate for these disappointments, particularly the disappointment over the proposed heavy water plant. Once again I strongly urge the ministers concerned to take serious cognizance of these remarks.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Another matter it is pertinent to mention at this time is Expo '67, which is referred to so often in the House of Commons and of which we are so proud as part of our centennial celebrations. During the Christmas holiday I had the pleasure of visiting our great sister nation to the south for a couple of weeks. I was relatively far south for a period of a week or two. When I mentioned our centennial celebrations and used the phrase "Expo '67", no one seemed to know what I was talking about. They said, "What does that mean?" They were not familiar with the expression. On the contrary, when I spoke of the world fairs at Brussels or Seattle or the recent one in New York city, they knew what I was talking about. It was necessary for me to go to some length to explain that Canada is celebrating its one hundredth birthday and that as a part of the celebration we are developing what we hope will be one of the greatest world fairs in history.
Just a few days ago, during a discussion on a C.B.C. program, the point again was brought home to Canadians that we are not selling Expo '67 in the proper manner. I am not saying this with the intention to disparage the officials of Expo. I believe most of us in the House of Commons, because we are adjacent to the area, are very well aware of what Expo '67 is and are looking forward to attending this great exhibition. I am thinking, however, of the economic welfare of Canada and the population as a whole.
I am sorry the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) is not in the house. I believe he should take a serious look at this situation to see whether emphasis should be put on the words "Canada's World Fair" instead of the words "Expo 67". The expression "world's fair" amplifies the importance of the event. This is something about which I believe all of us should be concerned. I was very disappointed and concerned when I learned of the lack of knowledge on the part of a great many people who live farther south, people whom we hope will visit us in large numbers this year. They did not know what I was talking about when I used this terminology.

Recently, of course, we have been interested in what has been going on closer to home. This brings me back to the budget and finances, as well as the row over the Mercantile Bank. The principal points involved in the Stevens-Coyne-Westbank-British International Finance dispute are set forth in a recent issue of the Financial Post. I believe it would be worth while to quote this editorial for the record because I am in agreement with the opinion stated therein in respect of this matter. This is what the Financial Post has to say about this dispute:
In 1964, the Porter royal commission on banking and finance, appointed by the Diefenbaker government, recommended that Canada should not allow control of Canadian banks to fall into foreign hands. It was concerned about the grave concentration of power that might shift outside Canada, particularly to New York.
Canada is not the only country which has faced this problem. Britain hasn't much formal organizational control through legislation but it has immense influence in practice over the conduct of foreign financial institutions. In France, licensing of a foreign bank is subject to the discretion of the government. Japan insists that at least 50 per cent of the stock of all corporations, including banks, must be owned by Japanese, and has extensive controls on foreign exchange and capital movements.
Denmark, Sweden, Spain, Australia, South Africa all arrange, one way or another, to set limits on foreign banks.
Even in the U.S., only six states or areas- Washington, Oregon, California, New York, Puerto Rico and Virgin Islands-specifically permit foreign banking and none permits a complete range of banking service.
Canadian policy, at the time First National City Bank was buying Mercantile, was clearly aimed at keeping control of Canadian banks within Canada. If there was any doubt, Canada's finance minister personally made this policy plain to the Citibank people. He didn't have to warn them, but it was surely in their interest that he did so.
Washington charges that Ottawa is discriminating against U.S. banks. But the new ownership rules are being applied to the Canadian owned banks as well as to the Mercantile. All Canadian banks will have an upper limit of 25 per cent foreign ownership now, and a limit of 10 per cent in any one foreign holder's hands.
No small nation could have a better big next door neighbour than Canada has, and Americans have reason to feel lucky that they have a bountiful friendly Canada close by.
Unfortunately, the Mercantile dispute involves an issue on which Ottawa can't back down.
The U.S. banks accept local restrictions in other countries. Perhaps Washington will have the good sense to realize that Canada's stand is reasonable.
In my opinion, this puts in a nutshell the general thinking of most Canadians. I do not always agree with the policy of the government in respect of economic matters, but here
February 10, 1967	COMMONS
is one instance in which I do agree with them. I think the Financial Post puts this whole matter into proper perspective.
Another matter about which I am concerned has to do with our economic welfare. I am thinking now of western Canada and the proposed increase in the St. Lawrence seaway tolls. I was very interested to receive from the Great Lakes Waterways Development Association a copy of a speech made by Mr. Paul Yakabuski, M.P.P. for Renfrew South, in the Ontario legislature quite recently. I think this more or less exemplifies the feeling of the people in western Canada as well as the feeling of the people of Ontario about this matter. I should like to quote a few excerpts because I think it puts forward my views even more effectively than I could.
When the costs of moving such essential bulk commodities as coal, iron ore, limestone and petroleum products to the industrial heart of Canada go up, a very unfavourable influence is exerted upon the economy of this province.
Higher power and raw material costs to primary manufacturers mean higher costs and prices of semi-finished products to secondary manufacturers. Hence, the cost of Ontario finished goods to wholesale and retail distributors in all parts of Canada go up; and this multiplier effect is reflected in prices to consumers in every part of this country.
In similar fashion, the costs and prices of Canadian natural and manufactured products destined for foreign markets go up, thereby lessening the ability of producers throughout the Canadian economy to compete in the ever more competitive world market.
It is for those reasons that the province of Ontario, along with the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan-
I should like to re-emphasize this, because it is equally effective in, and pertains to, the western provinces.
It is for those reasons that the province of Ontario, along with the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan, opposed the seaway toll and Welland ship canal lockage charges recommendations of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority at the toll hearings held in Ottawa on May 25th and 26th last year.
It is interesting to note the following;
Of the 58 submissions with respect to its recommendations presented to the Seaway Authority at the Ottawa toll hearings last year, only two were in favour of the recommended increase in seaway tolls, and the imposition of lockage charges on the Welland ship canal.
But despite the opposition of the Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan governments, and of very highly qualified and responsible organizations, to the toll and lockage charges recommendations; and despite a unique debate in the House of Commons on May 26, 1966, inspired by that overwhelming opposition, when members of all five of our political parties including four courageous members of the
The Budget-Mr. Southam Liberal party, opposed the recommendations, the Seaway Authority has ignored all the submissions.
I spoke on this matter during the debate in the month of May last year. At that time I emphasized, and I emphasize again, that if these tolls are imposed the people in western Canada will be faced with a double impost because the tolls will affect the shipment of their grain to eastern markets through the St. Lawrence seaway. Eastern Canada is the heart of our industrial area. This is where all the heavy goods such as cars, machinery, refrigerators and so on are manufactured. These goods are shipped through the seaway to the head of the lakes and then through the great area of the west which is not heavily populated and now will have no bridge subsidy formerly payable on goods shipped by rail through northern Ontario. By the time these products reach our markets in western Canada the penalty of any increase imposed in the St. Lawrence system is doubled or tripled. I implore the minister to consider our recommendations not to increase these tolls.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The article to which I referred makes reference to the courage displayed by Liberal members who have spoken in opposition to this measure. This should be an indication to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) that he should look seriously at this policy before making a final decision.
Let me reiterate something said by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand), and touched upon by another of my colleagues, the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Kennedy), regarding education. The greatest resource in Canada is not gold in the ground, wheat in the field, minerals or forest products, but rather the human resource.
It was interesting and rather disconcerting to read Dr. Deutsch's report on education in Canada and how it affects our productivity. This is something about which we should be concerned during this centennial year. We should try to assist our provinces in turn to provide assistance at the primary, secondary and university levels of education in order that we may utilize to the maximum degree the potential ability of our population.
I was interested in an article written by Dr. Spinks, president of the University of Saskatchewan, who was quoted in the following terms;
"Contrary to a widely held belief, our average educational level is considerably behind that in the United States. In 1961, only 6 per cent of the whole working force in Canada held a university


The Budget-Mr. Southam degree compared with 11 per cent in the United States. About 25 per cent in Canada had four years of high school compared to 50 per cent in the U.S."
This same article also states that-
-Dr. Spinks referred to a 1961 National Research Council report which said that unless Canada as an industrial power is content to remain inferior to the U.S. and the United Kingdom, a way must be found to induce industry to devote more of its resources to research.
Another paragraph of the article reads as follows:
Noting the emphasis placed by recent economic studies on "the overriding influence of education" in increasing the gross national product, Dr. Spinlcs said, "it is not just chance that for many years Canadian productivity has been only 70 per cent of that of the United States".
Dr. Spinks said it was not just chance that productivity has been only 70 per cent of that in the United States, but because our standard of education has not been developed on a basis similar to the one in that great country. These facts should weigh heavily on our minds, and the authorities responsible for alleviating this situation should adopt as a centennial project-

Thank you. A survey was conducted a number of years ago in the province of Saskatchewan regarding the relationship between education and income. At that time the average income there was approximately $5,000 per year. That was approximately ten years ago. That survey was based on a productive life expectancy of 40 years, from age 20 to 60. On that basis the average individual would contribute something in the neighbourhood of $200,000 to society over a period of 40 years.
Using that as an example it seems to me that we could enhance our productivity by increasing average annual salaries to $6,000 or $7,000. This can only be done by developing the potential capacity of individuals through higher education. About 30 years

ago Saskatchewan had a population of roughly 850,000. It gradually increased to about 860,000, but then started to decrease because of automation in agriculture and an unfavourable political climate. The people in Saskatchewan desire to enjoy the same standards of services and education as are enjoyed by other areas of Canada. Because of this decrease in population the tax load was borne by a smaller number of citizens. This resulted in a very high tax structure. It is imperative that we maintain some even distribution of population and industry. We must improve our educational system as quickly as possible in order to obtain a better balanced economy.
Some months ago a very interesting article appeared in the Weekend Magazine regarding secondary education in schools of the nonacademic type. The minister of labour in the former Progressive Conservative administration the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) realized that one of the basic causes of unemployment in this country was lack of knowledge or specialized training. As a result of his efforts our vocational and educational trade school program was developed. Very few people realize what this program has done to increase our productivity and economic strength. We have been happy to note that the present government has not cut back on this program, although there has been some indication that it may place more of this load on provincial governments. Vocational training is something that should be emphasized throughout Canada, because not everyone can become a professional. This is an age of specialization and we must have people trained in specialized fields.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the government to consider seriously the comments which have been made, particularly those in respect of the province of Saskatchewan. Any improvement in the economy of that province will naturally be reflected by a general improvement in the economic welfare of this country.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I wish to deal with one major issue. It is an issue that is not new to this house and is one about which I am sure we will hear much more in the ensuing months. I am particularly glad that the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) is in her seat this afternoon, because I am hopeful that these words will provide some impetus or motivation, particularly on the part
February 10, 1967	COMMONS
of her department, with regard to what I consider to be a critical problem in our country today. This is a problem related to the whole sphere of political action and political responsibility, not only in respect of those who are elected representatives or civil servants, but people generally.
Perhaps because I am a freshman member of parliament some of my reaction to the systems by which we govern ourselves will be considered rather bold. Perhaps, in some senses of the word, they will be even naive. But one of the things that has never ceased to amaze me since becoming a member of parliament is the very close relationship that exists between those of us who work on this floor and those who occupy the press gallery. It is that crucial relationship, indeed, that establishes some kind of rapport and understanding in the country for what politics and political action are all about. When that relationship breaks down or becomes confused, not only does parliament suffer but I think the whole process of self-government suffers greatly.
One of the things that has continued to concern me very much about this whole question is the fact that we have invoked in our political processes and parliamentary activity a kind of discrimination that I think would not be tolerated for one moment in any other sphere of human activity. We have continued to acquiesce in this discrimination, to allow it to be accepted, almost without question, until we have given a kind of preferential treatment to one aspect of the mass media of communication and discriminated against the rest. I think that part of the problem of relating the process that takes place in this house to people generally is faulty and inadequate communication. Marshall McLuhan would put it this way, I suppose, that we have moved from the era of print to one of the electronic age in which now it is possible for people to become, almost quite literally, plugged-in on the important events of our civilization. I believe that in our time we have seen this most uniquely and clearly when events of great national and international significance have taken place.
I do not believe it would ever have been possible in any previous era for a whole continent, and one might say almost the whole of a civilization, to become related as one community to the events in Dallas and Washington on a particular week end in 1963, had it not been for the availability of television. Television transformed what was a national
The Budget-Mr. D. MacDonald and somewhat localized event into an international, indeed almost universal, experience. We also have the further experience that continues to take place from time to time of the occasional satellite attempts, particularly by the United States, to which immediate access is given by television to millions of viewers.
We have had events of national significance in our country over the past few years, but they have not commonly been available to people in some of their most important points because we have exerted a kind of media discrimination. This discrimination is not something that began this year or last year, but rather it has been going on for a number of years and has been tolerated almost without comment by nearly everyone.
So I speak out for a new understanding of the nature and uses of mass media and ask that they not be used to expose for purposes of power or popularity any individual in this house or outside it, but to create a more genuine, a more thoughtful and a more purposeful dialogue between our activity in the house and the thoughts and desires of the nation. I think it has been interesting to observe over the past few weeks the reaction of many people-it has been almost general across the country-to one of the most recent television dramas of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I refer to the Quentin Durgens program. I wonder whether hon. members have thought, as I have, why this program so immediately created an interest on the part of people living all across this country.
I am sure that many members of this house have discovered in their travels to their constituencies that this popular program, which was on the television screen for the short period of seven or eight weeks, established a whole new series of thoughts and considerations and, perhaps what is even more important, sympathy for those who labour within the confines of parliament. Perhaps we could say that one of the reasons was that it was a very good drama, that the writer George Robertson and the producer David Gardner were men of exceptional ability and were able to provide us with good television entertainment. I believe there was more to this program than entertainment, because time and time again it has been made quite clear to me by many friends and neighbours that here, for the first time, people who had never had the opportunity of coming to grips with


The Budget-Mr. D. MacDonald parliament were able to get inside, to understand strange and baffling terms like "caucus", "party whips" and "parliamentary committees". They were able to understand even in some minor way what they meant. I think this is crucial.
If there has been cynicism, and there has, on the part of many as to the effectiveness of our parliamentary process today, I think this one, short television series did more to dispel it than any other single thing in modern day experience. This program taught us a lesson, I hope, that we have in our systems of mass communication, radio and television, an unparalleled opportunity to greatly facilitate and make much more effective our whole program of self-government. I think it is tragic that we have for so long barred the door against these two important media and exercised a kind of discrimination in this respect.
I am told that a number of years ago when radio first became significant in our country, the only reporters allowed in the press gallery were those who were providing written reports for newspapers, magazines and journals; but of course some of the radio systems wanted to have access to what was going on in parliament and I am told they made application to become members of the press gallery.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Somehow it seemed odd and strange to allow these people who were not writing the news, but speaking it, to be given that access, and therefore in the early years those who provided news for the radio waited outside the press gallery, and when some member came out they asked him questions to find out what had been going on inside. This seems ridiculous to us today. I do not think that anyone would rise in his place in the house and demand that all those who report for radio and television should be kept out of the press gallery. But we do. I know we allow them to come in physically to write down what they hear or what they see, but when it comes to someone recording either on film or on tape the events which take place in the house, objections are raised as if this would almost defile this house. I think that this is a tragic misreading of the opportunities which both the radio and television provide to us in this electronic era.
It seems strange also, when politicians are so inclined to look for precedents for actions, that we are more than willing to ignore a number of precedents both in our system and

in other countries that have made available to the mass media the great forums for decision making and legislative action.
A few years ago when I was travelling in Australia I remember being able to tune in the radio at any point in that country and hear at that very moment what great matters of state were being discussed in their legislative chambers. It seemed to me a great thing. I am not sure whether the audiences there are very large, in fact I believe that the reverse is true, but the opportunity is there, and that is of immeasurable value.
I am not so much concerned about this chamber specifically but about the various urgent, important and interesting matters that are being discussed in our committees. Surely this has been a year in which it would have been more than interesting to have live reports, video taped records or tape recorded reports of the various committee discussions such as perhaps the discussions which are going on this very afternoon in the defence committee, those that dealt earlier with the problems of the Mercantile Bank, or more recently the altercation between Mr. Coyne and Mr. Stevens, or even earlier in this session the long discussions over the "Seven Days" controversy. I am sure there was a great deal of public interest for all these matters, and yet in each and every one of these committees the cameras were treated as if they were some kind of furtive alien.
In some instances the television camera was poised outside the committee room door, lurking as if it were some kind of an unwanted interloper, and occasionally when the opportunity arose, glimpsing some picture within. And yet, sitting at the very front desk in each committee, was the press, writing, if they wished, every single word that was expressed in that committee and also adding for the benefit of the reader any particular emotional expressions or nuances that might not be expressed in the verbalized word.
I cannot understand why, when we have encompassed so much that is modern and new in our technology, we have continued to exercise a kind of prejudice against the visual and the aural, because it is true as true can be that the major decisions of people that are being made with respect to the whole of the democratic process are largely being made in response to what they have seen on the television screen, or what they have heard on the radio. Indeed if we were to take a survey I am sure that we would discover that the great majority of our population today spends
February 10, 1967	COMMONS
so much time watching television-well over 20 hours a week on the average-that this is their great forum of communication.
In spite of this we have effectively blocked year after year the availability to people of what is happening in this place. I think we have done a great disservice to parliament, and even more than that we have done a great disservice to the people of this country.
This matter has been raised on a number of occasions during the present session, and at this point I would like to remind the house of what has been said, and of the understanding which we now have on this matter. On one of the earliest occasions in this session, on May 4, 1966, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), in discussing the questions related to the establishment of quorums in the house and in committees, said the following, as recorded on page 4675 of Hansard:
I have on more than one occasion-and this is an opportunity to raise this matter again-expressed the view that if we wish to restore parliament so the people will understand its operations, one means to bring that about would be through broadcasts or television representation of parliament from day to day. I can tell you, sir, that if this practice were adopted in committees as an experiment there would be no difficulty about having a full quorum in committees at all times.
It has been argued sometimes that to introduce these dangerous communication instruments of radio and television into this house and into committees would cause many hon. members who sit here faithfully day after day to simply sit in their offices, or wherever they might be, and watch television or listen over the radio to what was taking place in the house. Anyone who makes that kind of a statement does not understand the nature of these media and, even more more than that, does not understand the nature of politicians, for I have found very few politicians-and these were not politicians for very long-who were anxious to run away continually from these media and, even more than that, very reverse would be true, as the right hon. gentleman remarked. If we introduced these mass media into this house we might indeed find that more members would be sitting here during the debates, and in fact it might indeed be difficult to extract them to their offices or to committee meetings, where they have to be from time to time.
On Thursday, November 10, 1966 the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather), in dealing with the same matter, asked the 23033-817J
The Budget-Mr. D. MacDonald Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) the following question:
I have a question for the Secretary of State, Mr. Speaker. Will the minister consider doing what the British government is doing at this time in respect of a study regarding the televising of the proceedings of parliament?
And the minister answered:
I had the opportunity this summer of observing what is being done and contemplated in this regard in Australia, New Zealand, Italy and Britain. I am informed that Mr. Speaker on behalf of the House of Commons has made a very detailed study of the U.K. experience and plans to telecast in this regard.
This might be a question about which, under the estimates to which they are related-those for the B.B.G. and C.B.C.-the broadcasting committee might well decide to hear witnesses and to discuss this matter. It will be remembered, however, that when such a motion was placed before that committee to televise the committee proceedings during the Seven Days matter, it was rejected. Perhaps Mr. Speaker on behalf of all members will discuss this matter with the broadcasting committee on the basis of that information which I am sure he now has.
An interesting footnote to the comment by the Secretary of State-and of course her information on the first decision of the broadcasting committee was correct-was that at a later date this fall the committee reversed its recommendation and indeed recommended to Mr. Speaker that broadcasting of committees be attempted on an experimental basis.
A further question was raised on the same matter by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition on November 30, 1966 when he asked the following question:
Now that the question of television in the British parliament has been dealt with by a free vote of the British House of Commons sn a motion moved for the purpose, would the Prime Minister consider having a motion placed before the house, free of the whips, to provide for television in this house? I suggest that it might be done on an experimental basis to start with so as to allow us in the house to decide whether it is appropriate at present and in the public interest that an opportunity be given to the Canadian people to see parliament in action. Such a move also would enable Canadians to appreciate better than they otherwise can the operation of this institution.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important question of course and I will be very glad to give it my consideration along the lines indicated by my right hon. friend.
Unfortunately, that was on November 30 last and we have had no further indication in this house as to what action might be taken. I


The Budget-Mr. D. MacDonald have been heartened from time to time, Mr. Speaker, by the comments of the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Turner), who has in two or three public speeches made remarks to the effect we are moving in the direction of understanding when we permit the accessibility of radio and television to our parliamentary activities.
Finally, I should like to read some letters which form part of the evidence of the broadcasting committee. The first letter is from the chairman of the broadcasting committee to Mr. Speaker and it reads:
I am instructed by the standing committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts to convey to you the committee's opinion that consideration should be given to radio and television broadcasting of a committee's proceedings on an experimental basis. Enclosed for your information is a copy of the twelfth report of the committee's subcommittee on agenda and procedure which was adopted by the committee at its meeting last night.
The Speaker's reply reads as follows:
This will acknowledge your letter of December 13 in which you bring to my attention the recommendations contained in the report of your subcommittee on agenda and procedure.
I am sure you share my doubts as to the committee's authority to submit recommendations regarding radio and television broadcasting of committee proceedings. Looking over the terms of reference of the standing committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts it would appear that it is not empowered by the house to consider the proposals contained in the subcommittee's report.
In my view authority to broadcast or telecast committee proceedings can only be given by the House of Commons itself and I, as Speaker, cannot substitute my judgment for that of the house in this regard.
This would seem to leave the matter squarely in the hands of this place. It is my urgent hope that the government, and more particularly the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), will bring this matter before the house this year. We have talked in a very grandiose way of the great things we are going to do in 1967. Everyone has been making so many comments that it has become almost a standing joke as to what your own particular centennial project will be. Surely, along with the many other things we have set aside for ourselves to do as worthy projects on this 100th birthday, there is one we might consider for parliament itself. We should make a real attempt to make accessible to the people of Canada what we do in this place. I think if we adopt an enlightened, realistic attitude to the nature and purpose of the mass media we will effect some changes here of real importance.

We will look to the extension of opportunity in this house and in committee for the radio and television media. I frankly think we have missed the boat time and again by denying the rights and privileges to radio and television which we have granted to the print media for 100 years now. Surely it is high time, in this centennial year, that we adopted the same fair attitude toward radio and television. There are many benefits to be gained by it, not the least of which I think is an enlightened public opinion. As every member of this house knows, little can be done in this place unless the public will it to be so. If we are anxious to increase the quality and effectiveness of the legislation that is passed by this house, that is discussed in the various committees, we will have no fear whatever of making available in our many forums complete accessibility to the media of radio and television.

might, Mr. Speaker, for a few moments I should like to follow along the same theme as the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald). I should like to make a few comments that appear to me to need to be said in so far as the image of parliament is concerned, and in so far as the great demand that seems to be pressing upon his institution to modernize its rules in such a way as to make what many feel has to be a more effective day to day working operation.
What concerns me, and has concerned me for some time, is that on many occasions in this forum we are asked to give up some of the rights we have as a legislative body and turn them over to the executive. More and more, the executive is becoming all-powerful and the legislative body less and less powerful. Whether you look at the problem of the separation of powers from the point of view of political science or philosophy, or whether you look at it on the basis of the day to day work of this institution as compared with the executive, I do not believe you will find there is a great deal of merit in the suggestions that are put forward.
In my opinion, this is a debating forum. This is the forum in which we try to get an expression of opinion from all corners of the house, from all parts of the nation, as to whether or not a given piece of legislation is of real benefit to the development of the nation. At the same time, we give careful consideration to the ways in which the taxpayers' money is being spent. So long as that is the main responsibility of this forum, I do not


believe we should tamper too much with the individual rights of members of parliament, nor do I believe we should greatly strengthen the already strong executive arm of government.
At the same time, I believe there is a responsibility to go into all the various areas of the economic spectrum in our committees. I do not believe this necessarily means we have to develop to a greater degree the kind of thing that seems to be developing in our committees system. For instance, at the moment we have a large body of members who belong to a certain committee of this house away in another part of the nation taking a first-hand look at a certain problem. I do not believe there is anything wrong with committees travelling, if first-hand information is going to be of value. However, I do not believe you need 30 or 40 members away looking at this particular problem. I do not believe the money spent carrying out such a project is really necessary, and I believe our committees ought to be a good deal smaller. At the same time if we spend money, making available to this smaller group of members a greater research capability, we shall be in a better position to get from them a better judgment. They will be able to judge whether the government is approaching a matter properly.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We could learn a great deal from the United States committees system. Studying the congressional committees system of the United States would be money well spent, especially if two or three men could do a job, instead of having large bodies of members having to travel over the country.
The present committees system of the House of Commons is unfair to committee members. Ministers, arguing for their legislation come before committees with batteries of individuals who prepared the legislation, studied the problem in detail, and who tell the group of committee members why the legislation ought to be approved in that particular form. In the end the members of parliament are brainwashed. Who are they, to argue with the battery of professionals? The individual members have other responsibilities. They can do research work, but their time and financial resources are limited. The resources of the country are available to the minister who wants his legislation approved. It is almost impossible, under the present system, for legislation not to be approved.
The Budget-Mr. Coates
Let us take a look at the situation as it exists. Twenty four or more committees are sitting, most with a quorum of 20 or more members. If all the committees should meet at the same time nobody would sit in the house. Yet, when people come to this chamber they look down and say: "My goodness, onty 20 or 25 members are in the chamber. Where are the rest of them, who have been elected to this institution?" Parliament is given a black eye because the public does not understand that a member may be doing something outside the chamber which he feels is important to his constituents. All too often the impression is that members are away.
When the bells ring for a vote you find, suddenly, that 100 members appear to vote for something. All I say is that in any given time too many committees make too many demands on the available members. Another thing not considered is that, though 265 members are elected to this chamber, 27 are cabinet ministers, a few more are parliamentary secretaries, and some others are involved in the operation of the house. Less than 265 members therefore are available for committee work.
Ministers and parliamentary secretaries are involved in the day to day operations of government and cannot be available for other duties. The number of members available to serve on the 24 committees becomes smaller and-I am looking at the Liberal whip-the whips of the parties have an awful time rounding up members for committees, or to form a quorum in the chamber. Yet the public, looking at the chamber and seeing 25 members, say, "Well, that's parliament for you." Often we cannot explain to the public what a member of parliament does outside the chamber.
If you cut the number of committee members down and gave every member of the house the right to ask questions of any committee with the consent of the chairman, and if you gave research assistance to those serving on committees, you would soon find that experts would develop in the various fields of government. They need not be members of the government.
I must mention something else. When you come to Ottawa, especially if you are a young man and ambitious, you will find that besides intelligence and aggressiveness, religion, where you come from and many other things will determine whether you will sit on the treasury benches-that is, assuming your party forms the government. We cannot do

February 10, 19B7
The Budget-Mr. Coates anything about that, but we can do this: We can make the position of a committeeman truly significant. We can arrange affairs so that, by spending time and energy, a man may become an expert in a field. If a minister came before a committee seeking approval of his legislation, his battery of experts would not in those circumstances brainwash the committee members. The minister would find himself confronted by men who know their subjects. Cabinet ministers in the United States are not elected, but they have to convince their committees, often composed of experts. In our country, if this suggestion were adopted, the minister would know that his legislation would be subject to educated, learned criticism.
Surely, if we left our rules alone, if we
stopped eroding the responsibilities of individual members and endeavoured to make our committees system more effective we would find that legislation returning to the chamber would secure a quicker passage than at present.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Where a committee is composed of, say, 20 men, the majority of them are government members concerned first and foremost with the government's image, whether in committee or in the house. They have at all times to be concerned about the government's image, whether in committee or in this house. The opposition members find great difficulty in amending the legislation. They must either approve or vote against it. So little progress is made before the legislation comes back to the house, and once again hon. members find themselves in the same position as before; I do not see that we are much further ahead.
I understand there is another committee which is supposed to leave in the course of the next two days and go in two directions, taking with it a large number of the members of the house. I do not see anything wrong about members getting across the country, talking to people and hearing different points of view. But I think we are sent here, basically, to do the countrys' business, and most of the country's business can be done here. Most of the groups which desire to make presentations to committees are financially capable of coming here and explaining their position.
On far too many occasions members are not as well equipped to understand these submissions as they would be if better research facilities were available to them. I have been down to Washington on more than one occasion on Canada-United States parliamentary

trips. What impressed me there was that when a congressman or a senator walked into a committee to discuss a subject he had either one or two men behind him, and when a question was referred to him he could turn to them and discuss it, very much as is done in this house when estimates are before us for consideration and the deputy minister, and other officials, are available to the minister for consultation. These men in Washington were capable of speaking on a great range of subjects in a very learned way, because they had the services of research assistants who could bring them up to date at all times on any subject.
If we are to have a more effective parliament we shall need more learned members of parliament. In my opinion there is nothing wrong with the I.Q. of any individual who can get himself elected to parliament; but it is one thing to have the I.Q., and another to be able to develop knowledge in many different fields. The complexity of government in Canada today as compared with 1867 is so great that, rather than saying "penny wise and pound foolish" we would be pound wise and penny foolish if we did not soon move into an area where we tried to assist all members of parliament, regardless of the party with which they are associated, by providing research facilities which would make them better able to understand and criticize whatever was being done. After all, the object of all members should be to produce the legislation which will bring the greatest amount of benefit to the Canadian nation, and this is one way in which this can be accomplished.
There are several ways and means of streamlining some of the rules of the house. For example, I do not see any great value in retaining any longer the resolution stage of bills. During the resolution stage we talk on the same subject as we debate when second reading is discussed. It is a duplication. While the present arrangement may have had merits at one time, I do not think any useful purpose is served by its continuation.
The arrangement for the question period has worked out very well. I was concerned about what might happen when this new idea of a limited question period was introduced, but I think it has worked to the satisfaction of all members of the house. However, there are some other suggested provisional rules which cause me concern. Certainly the rule with regard to the time allotted for a discussion of estimates causes me concern, because


we ended the last session without an opportunity-because of a choice made by the opposition-for having any kind of discussion on estimates, which represented a great deal of the money which was spent. I do not think this is of benefit to parliament in the long run.
If it is necessary to set a time limit-and I do not think it is, necessarily-I believe some time must be spent on all the departments, so that no department is allowed to pass unscanned, without any kind of surveillance by members.
There are other rules which might be streamlined. I do not think it is necessary for speeches to be as long as they are now. We could save time there. I do not know whether the debate on the speech from the throne, or the debate on the budget need to be as long as they are at present, though when we have a chamber composed of as many members as this one is, we must make sure there is reasonable opportunity for everyone to speak.

I have had to re-introduce the bill on April 8, 1965, and on January 24, 1966. I am happy that in February, 1967, it has been called for debate. I note an hon. member is applauding the speed of the cabinet in making it possible for the bill to come forward so fast.
I would like to state at the very first moment of moving second reading that the act which this bill seeks to repeal, chapter 266 of the revised statutes, entitled "An Act to Restrain the Use of Tobacco by Young Persons," is being broken every day that the House of Commons sits throughout the entire year. It is broken with the open consent of the members of the house and absolutely
Tobacco Restraint Act nothing is done about it. No charge is laid under the act.
I make this statement without any fear of contradiction because under this ridiculous chapter 266, an Act to Restrain the Use of Tobacco by Young Persons, any juvenile under the age of 16 who has cigarettes or cigarette papers in his possession at any time is guilty of an offence and can be convicted. Yet in the House of Commons we have a fine force of page boys, of whom the great majority are under age 16. The moment a juvenile buys the cigarettes not only is he guilty but the person selling them to him is guilty as well. But no charges are ever laid.

speechtext: Shame.

speechtext:
Yes, shame. The page boys bring the cigarettes back to the members and most of them retire, either behind the curtains or into the members' lobbies, and indulge in the pastime of smoking.
There are sections of this act, chapter 266, that cause offence to me and to those who have read it-and I am sorry to say that is a minority of the house-because under this act presumption can be the convicting force.
In section 2 of the act it is stated:
Every one is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction in the case of a first offence
to a penalty	who	sells....cigarettes or

.-to a juvenile; and then there are these words:
-which tobacco he knows or has reason to believe is for the use of that person.
How in the name of heaven can anybody tell what is in the mind of a tobacconist when he sells cigarettes or cigarette papers to a child under the age of 16? How do you know the tobacconist "has reason to believe" the child is going to use the tobacco?
Section 3 of the act goes on to point out:
It is the duty of any constable or person having the powers of a constable, or person authorized so to do by any by-law in that behalf made by any authority or person having power to make such by-law, to seize any cigarettes, cigarette papers or tobacco in any form other than cigarettes in the possession of any person apparently-

-note "apparently"-

under the age of 16 years whom he finds smoking or chewing-
And this is the stumbling block in the whole thing to which all members of the House of Commons must object-
-whom he finds smoking or chewing or about to smoke or chew tobacco in any street or public place.
How is anyone going to tell whether someone is about to smoke or chew tobacco just because he may have some in his possession? Mr. Speaker, I had a hard time in the city of Ottawa getting this plug of chewing tobacco which I hold in my hand.
