speechtext: So that is what we smell about you.

subtopic: REPEAL OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING USE BY JUVENILES
speechtext:
It is Sweet Briar. The fact that I have this plug of chewing tobacco in my possession and in my hand I can assure you is no assurance that I am about to chew it, but under this act it is an offence for a juvenile to be about to chew it, and I would like to find the police officer or crown attorney who can prove it.
Section 4 of the act returns to the child under the age of 16 and says of him:
-who, being under the age of 16 years... has in his possession, whether for his own use or not,-
And this is what covers the page boys here. -any cigarettes or cigarette papers-
-is guilty of an offence-
-and liable on summary conviction in the case of first offence to be reprimanded, in the case of a second offence to a penalty not exceeding one dollar, and in the case of a third or subsequent offence to a penalty not exceeding four dollars, who, being under the age of 16 years, smokes or chews tobacco in a street or public place, or purchases or has in his possession, whether for his own use or not-
These are the cigarettes the page boys are taking back to members.
-any cigarettes or cigarette papers, or purchases or has in his possession for his own use tobacco in any form other than cigarettes.
I draw this to the attention of the house to show how ridiculous the act is. The act was introduced in 1908, which is only 59 years ago, and there is not a recorded conviction under it. Why have the statute books been cluttered up with an act like this, which is 
ridiculous on the face of it, which presumes people to be guilty, and on top of that has never had a conviction under it in 59 years?
We come again to those under 16 years of age. Section 5 says:
If, on complaint to a justice, it is established to his satisfaction that an automatic machine, for the sale of cigarettes, cigars or tobacco in any form-
I might interpose, Mr. Speaker, that somebody has been kind enough to send me a cigar. It is a Simon Statesman. Thank you. I am glad it is not a "Politician"; and referring to the cigar I would like to jump for a moment from section 5 of the act to section 7 which says:
For the purposes of this act the word "cigarette" includes any small cigar made of tobacco rolled up in paper, tobacco leaf or any other material.
So, the act covers cigars as well.
To return to section 5, it says:
If, on complaint to a justice, it is established to his satisfaction that an automatic machine, for the sale of cigarettes, cigars or tobacco in any form, kept on any premises, is being used by persons under the age of 16 years, the justice may order the person on whose premises the machine is kept to take such precautions to prevent its being so used as are specified in the order, or, if necessary, to remove the machine within any specified time.
Now, down in the Chateau Laurier hotel, which is government property operated by the C.N.R., there is a cigarette vending machine in the front lobby, and it has this prissy statement on the face of it, "Sales of cigarettes to minors are forbidden by law." I watched that machine for a while the other evening when I was down there and you would be surprised at the number of young lads who came in and purchased cigarettes by putting the necessary funds in the slot, pressing the proper lever, and out popped the cigarettes.
No one was there to see whether they were under 16 years or not. The machine will sell to anybody. You just put in the proper amount of money and press the proper lever. How can you convict a machine for selling to minors when you cannot question the machine in court?
Section 5(3) reads as follows:
Any person upon whose premises there is any such machine may himself or by his agent seize any cigarettes, cigars or tobacco obtained from such machine and in the possession of any person apparently-
Note the word "apparently".
-under the age of 16 years using such machine or smoking or about to smoke such cigarettes, cigars or tobacco.

I would like someone to define just what is that state of smoking in which you find a juvenile "about to smoke such cigarettes, cigars or tobacco."
Then in section 8 you have in my opinion the most heinous part of the act:
For the purposes of this act any person who appears to the justice dealing with an information or complaint hereunder to be under the age of 16 years shall be presumed to be under that age unless it is shown by evidence that he is in fact over that age, and the provisions of the Criminal Code relating to the proof of the age of young persons apply to offences under this section.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Here we have an act which presumes a person to be under the age of 16, and if he has any tobacco in his possession for his own use or not, he is automatically guilty. These words which presume a person to be in a situation where he is automatically guilty go against my grain. This recalls to me only one thing; that is, the proceedings in this house in respect of section 98 as we knew it. All of us are aware of that nefarious section which in 1919 was introduced by the late Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, and which was known in Canada as the section relating to unlawful association. I am not one who was unfriendly toward the former Co-operative Commonwealth Federation or is unfriendly to the New Democratic Party. I have admired their stand on many questions for many years. I maintain that section 98 might still be on the statute books of Canada had it not been for the insistent demand of the late J. S. Woodsworth that the section be repealed and the continuous support that the Toronto Star gave to the demands that this be repealed. I take off my hat to Hon. Ernest Lapointe for his great efforts in this matter.
I have before me a photostatic copy of section 98 and also copies of sections 97A and 97B. Prior to 1919 the sections were 97A and 97B. Then when amendments were made in 1919 they came into the Criminal Code under the number 98. The first section is labelled "Unlawful Associations." In section 2 of that nefarious act we have:
Any property, real or personal, belonging or suspected to belong to an unlawful association-
Then in section 4 we have, with regard to any prosecutions under this section, the words:
*-if it be proved that the person charged has
(a) attended meetings of an unlawful association ... it shall be presumed, in the absence of any proof to the contrary, that he is a member of such unlawful association.
Tobacco Restraint Act
This was a miserable piece of legislation. Hon. Ernest Lapointe on April 23, 1928, in introducing a bill to kill this section stated:
A bill similar to this has been adopted by this house five times, and in each case it has been rejected by the other chamber.
He went on to point out the nefarious features of the act. In that debate Mr. Woodsworth, as reported at page 2308 of Hansard for April 23, 1928, refers to any property belonging to or suspected to belong to such an organization, and then makes the ringing declaration:
I have always entertained the idea that British justice presumes a man innocent until he is proved guilty. In this case the presumption is that he is guilty until he can prove himself innocent.
In this ridiculous tobacco bill of 1908 the child is presumed to be uder 16 years of age until he proves he is over. I would ask this house to agree to the repeal of this ridiculous piece of legislation. Machines are selling tobacco to anyone who can put money in the slot. We know children under 16 years of age are smoking. No convictions have ever been made under this act in 59 consecutive years.
In calling for the repeal of the act, I should like to read to you the explanatory notes, which were written by a more able person than myself:
The long title of the act which this bill purposes to repeal is: "An Act to restrain the use of Tobacco by Young Persons."
This legislation which has been on our statute books since 1908 has certainly not accomplished what it started out to do. No doubt its purpose was excellent but it has had a contrary effect to what was intended. Like all law which is a dead letter and is not observed it tends to bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
Furthermore it is vicious legislation in that it is an attempt at thought control for it provides punishment (section 3) for a juvenile "about to smoke or chew tobacco" and (in section 4) for a juvenile who "has in his possession, whether for his own use or not, any cigarettes etc."
Many people have been killed by blows from a hammer or an ax, perhaps it should be made a crime to be found in possession of one of those horrible instruments.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the members of the house to repeal this act. An Act to restrain the use of Tobacco by Young Persons, in the same manner this house repealed section 98 because under our system of justice a man is presumed to be innocent until proven guilty.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure many members of this house, and I think particularly members on


Tobacco Restraint Act
this side, regard the hon. member for York Humber (Mr. Cowan) as an intermittent source of entertainment and enlightenment. In my view he is rather like the light-enment. In my view he is ratherlike the lighthouse with the revolving light which between periods of darkness flashes out, illuminating the landscape and revealing usually its unattractive qualities.
In rising today a few words in respect of this bill, frankly I am of two minds whether I should support it or oppose it. As some hon. members may know, I am one of those in the house who has taken an interest in trying to encourage the government and the country to become aroused over the epidemic disease connected with cigarette addiction. From that point of view it might be supposed that I would naturally oppose any step which would repeal any legislation intended even to reduce or curtail cigarette smoking among our young people.
Imust say that I think so little of our existing Tobacco Restraint Act that two years ago I brought forward a bill to amend it, in the hope that we might be able to put some teeth into it and modernize it so that it will meet the modern conditions of 1967, rather than those of 1908, the year of its origin. Therefore, personally I do not very much care whether the bill the hon. member brings forward is successful, or whether the existing Tobacco Restraint Act is repealed or not. I believe it might be better to amend it rather than repeal it. At any rate, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words and to put some of my views on record concerning the very serious need in this country for better legislation on this subject.
The situation regarding cigarette smoking among our young people in the year 1967 is very different from what it was when this legislation was enacted in 1908. Today we have some 9,000 young people every month starting to smoke cigarettes. They do so partly as a result of the inducement-type advertising on television, radio and in the press. The Tobacco Restraint Act of 1908 has no control over that situation. Throughout the world we have health departments and health experts who have looked into the disease situation. They have all come to the same basic conclusion, that there is a proven link between cigarette smoking and lung cancer and heart disease.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Our own Canadian Department of National Health and Welfare has done great work in recent years in this sphere. Early this week it

released another report underlining the link between cigarette smoking and heart disease. In spite of these educational efforts by health departments, the epidemic of cigarette smoking, with its attendant ill health, continues.
Perhaps it would be appropriate to quote from what has been said on this subject by a medical man of another country. The chief medical officer of the ministry of health in Great Britain said this, as reported in the New Statesman of January 20, 1967:
The increase will go on so long as these undoubted causes of death and illness are sold to a gullible public. Lung cancer and chronic bronchitis, the legacies of cigarette smoking, are not idle threats conjured up in these reports. They are the causes of five times as many deaths as follow road accidents in a year; yet they excite far less comment.
He was, of course, referring to cigarettes.
I should like also to quote very briefly from a United States authority, R. T. Ravenholt, as reported in the August-September issue last year of the National Newsletter. He said:
The "cigarette disease" has been described ... as the foremost preventable cause of death in the United States. He stated that for the American male aged 35 to 65 who smokes 20 or more cigarettes a day, tobacco is a hazard to life which is equal to all other hazards combined.
It is known that 80 per cent to 90 per cent of all lung cancers occur among smokers of cigarettes and more recently it has been recognized that the smoker has an increased risk of dying prematurely of other types of cancer, of heart disease or of chronic chest disease.
It is refreshing to find some progress being made in the combat against the cigarette disease. In England for ten months, there has been no television advertising promoting cigarettes. Quite recently in the United States the New Yorker has joined the Reader's Digest in refusing to carry cigarette advertising. In Canada we find that the government on the one hand spends money to discourage young people from smoking, yet on the other accepts revenue through tobacco taxation. It spends a great deal of money in the development of better types of tobacco. These things all take place at the same time.
Our government continually declines to request the C.B.C. to set an example by refusing to promote cigarette consumption through advertising. No matter how our legislation is worded, as the hon. member has suggested, and no matter how active is our educational work in this health field, we cannot succeed in preventing a great number of our children and young people from beginning to smoke, until we take some legislative step to Stop it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very brief and to the point. I support the comments of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather) regarding the use of tobacco and the dangers presently faced by our young people who become addicted to smoking. This house owes a debt to the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) because of his ability to ferret out these inadequate and redundant pieces of legislation. Certainly the act the hon. member seeks to repeal has no practical use. I am sure no one in the house could find any reason for allowing it to remain on our statute books.
Like the hon. member for New Westminster, and the hon. member for York-Humber, I do not use tobacco. I also believe that if we really intend to do something about curbing the use of tobacco we should do away with the Tobacco Restraint Act and start from the beginning to draft an act to deal effectively with the problems associated with smoking.
It would be a fine gesture at this time to give unanimous consent to this motion to repeal this act, which is chapter 26 of the Revised Statues of Canada, 1952, thus removing it from our statute books. To this end I earnestly plead to hon. members of this house to support the bill.

subtopic: REPEAL OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING USE BY JUVENILES
speechtext:
Tobacco Restraint Act goes out, but it leaves a coating on the inside of the lungs and cannot but harm the person who smokes this many cigarettes. Any athlete will tell you that if he becomes a heavy smoker he immediately becomes short-winded. Why is this? It is because the bloodstream does not receive the amount of oxygen it needs to function properly.
It does not matter whether the cigarette is filter tipped or not, you still inhale this amount of tar. You can make your own test with handkerchief or Kleenex; you will find tar is inhaled. If you start smoking at the age of 10, 12 or 13 it is not long before your lungs are clotted with tar. Anyone who starts smoking at this age has never given the lungs a chance to absorb oxygen normally.
I stress that if these are the effects, and they are scientifically proven and medically accepted, the government should take a very serious look at this question and make whatever changes are necessary, as suggested by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan). The hon. member set out his arguments very clearly and has taken the initiative of introducing this bill to repeal the Tobacco Restraint Act. That act should be removed from the statute books altogether, because it is absolutely useless as it stands, or repealed, as is suggested in this bill.
If the government is concerned about the health of the people of this country, not only with regard to water pollution, air pollution and things of that kind, but because of the smoking that goes on under our noses every day, this problem should be looked into and we must see whether legislation can be enacted that will fulfil the hopes of the government in regard to national health. The government should look into this whole problem, if it is to achieve what it hopes to achieve in improving the health of Canadians.
The hon. member for York-Humber has brought this matter to the attention of the house and the departmental officials responsible in this area. I hope the government will take action to remedy the situation and that the efforts of the hon. member for York-Humber and other hon. members of the house who are anxious to see a solution to this problem will not prove to be wasted. I hope this matter is not just on the record so that people can say, "On February 10, 1967, the house spoke on this matter" and we will find ourselves facing the same situation in 1987. The government should take action in this regard. I congratulate the hon. member for

York-Humber for having brought this question to the attention of the house.

subtopic: REPEAL OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING USE BY JUVENILES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I must congratulate the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois) for his excellent statement on pulmonary biology and physiology. I knew he was a professor of mathematics but I was not aware of his talents where human physiology is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I now rise to take part in the debate as a medical doctor, and also as one who has seen several patients suffer from lung cancer because of their immoderate, and even moderate, use of tobacco.
After reading this bill I felt it my duty to make a few remarks. This private bill proposes the repeal of the whole of chapter 266 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, that is the Tobacco Restraint Act.
I need not define the word tobacco. We know it comes from an indigenous American language. It belongs to the solanaceae family, which is native of Tobago, and whose leaves can be smoked, snuffed or chewed in various preparations. Let us say, incidentally, to make a long story short, that tobacco is a vigorous, strong, pleasure-giving and habit-forming plant that may grow as high as two metres, and has large leaves. Probably native of the Caribbean, it was imported into Europe by the Spanish and popularized by France, thanks to the ambassador of Catherine de Medici, Jean Nicot. It is now grown in almost every country. It is all the more dangerous as it is mainly grown in Cuba.
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure I share the views of my friend from York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) on the desirability of removing or repealing altogether the act to restrain the use of tobacco by young persons.
Several antiquated laws should be removed from the Criminal Code, I am sure. Yet, in many cases, a law, by its mere presence, has a deterrent or, to use a medical term, a prophylactic effect. If the presence of some laws in a few statute books succeeds in preventing certain offences, I am sure this particular piece of legislation could be used as medical prophylaxis, that is, to prevent people from starting the sad and bad habit of cigarette smoking at an age when they should refrain from doing so.
I agree with my colleague that this particular measure seems stupid. But such a


legislation is often necessary to make individuals, especially young people, behave decently, which they would not do otherwise. Having a father and mother has often prevented teenagers from misbehaving, simply because they thought of their parents or possibly of the authority the parents represent.
I am convinced that, more than ever, it is necessary to feel such authority, whatever its source, in order to have respect for it.
I was speaking of prevention a while ago, Mr. Speaker. There has been considerable study carried out on the subject and more is still being done. But there is one indisputable fact and it is that we are now almost sure that tobacco is a cause of lung cancer.
If we compare the higher death rate among male smokers with that from other causes, it will be noted that lung cancer accounts for 21 per cent of deaths, heart and blood vessel diseases account for 22.2 per cent, coronary diseases for 36.6 per cent, other cancers for 11.9 per cent, other causes for 2.4 per cent, and accidents, poisonings and violent deaths for 2.9 per cent. It is obvious from this that the Canadian people should definitely be brought to realize the dangers of nicotine. And the danger is even greater for cigarette smokers.
Let us look around a bit, if you will. First of all, chances of a cure, in the case of lung cancer, remain very slim, in spite of irradiation and radical surgery. Therefore, prevention rather than treatment should be insisted upon.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Let us take for example coronary diseases. In 1962, arteriosclerosis, the most frequent coronary disease, was the primary cause of death in Canada, having been responsible for the death of 25,549 men and 13,683 women. Cigarette smoking is related to an increase in the mortality rate from coronary disease, particularly among middle-aged men.
Several surveys have demonstrated the existence of a close connection between smoking and death caused by coronary disease. One need only look up page 32 of the report of the Royal College of Medicine and read the American report published on this subject. The mortality rate from coronary disease is higher among cigarette smokers than among non-smokers.
Studies have shown that the mortality rate for cigarette smokers is 1.7 per cent higher than for non-smokers, that the mortality rate due to coronary disease is directly related to the number of cigarettes a person smokes in one day, and that the mortality rate is even
Tobacco Restraint Act higher among middle-aged smokers, as compared with non-smokers.
The results of another study show that, for men between 40 and 49 years of age, the mortality coefficient is 3.9 per cent; then, the coefficient goes down to 2.1 per cent, 1.5 per cent and 1.3 per cent respectively, using ten-year age groups as a basis for comparison. Therefore, there is greater chance of death by coronary disease among middle-aged inveterate smokers.
It may therefore be said that the number of deaths due to coronary disease is lower among those who quit smoking cigarettes, as compared with those who did not.
The following statement may please some hon. members: the mortality rate due to coronary disease among pipe and cigar smokers is the same as that for non-smokers, which now stands at approximately 1 per cent.
The Dominion Bureau of Statistics reports that the following related diseases, namely chronic bronchitis or, if you would, chronic asthma and emphysema -which also lead to respiratory troubles, caused 1,197 deaths in Canada in 1962.
Studies on the expected effects of cigarette smoking on men reveal that the number of deaths caused by chronic bronchitis, chronic asthma and emphysema is higher with smokers than non-smokers.
There is no doubt that those who suffer from chronic bronchitis or emphysema cough themselves hoarse every morning, especially after having smoked a cigarette on an empty stomach, as shown by the popular expression which many patients use when they come to see us: "Doctor, every morning I almost spit my heart out."
This irritating phenomenon is most conclusive, and it certainly contributes to causing lung cancer. Yet, coughing and spitting are not nearly as common with old smokers as they are with those continue to smoke in general. One needs only refer to the chronic cough of coughers, or smokers' cough, as it is commonly called.
There is improvement when victims of broncho-pulmonary diseases quit smoking. Mr. Speaker, the one who now speaks to you quit smoking almost eight years ago. I may have put on a little weight but, even at that, I feel very fit. I can say that in the morning I feel as gay as a lark. I am no longer, Mr. Speaker, a slave to the cigarette.
It is also true that inveterate smokers always keep in their lungs as much as 50 per


Tobacco Restraint Act cent of the smoke inhaled. A few drops are deposited directly onto the walls of the bronchia, others are picked up by mobile cells mostly in the air sacks; several of the cells emigrate into the bronchia and travel up the walls of the membrane. We also note that the breathing capacity is inhibited in smokers.
It has been proved that those who begin smoking at an early age are short of breath, particularly when doing physical exercise or engaging in certain sports such as hockey, ski or basketball. Moreover, it has been established that cigarette smoke inhibits certain functions of the normal respiratory system, as I have just shown. It has also been noticed-and this is very serious-that a cerebral pollution occurs, causing a certain haze on the brain of the inveterate smoker, who will often put forward obscure and not too clear arguments, resulting in a foggy October morning type of reasoning. This is important for us, in this chamber, for we often feel the lunatic and confusing effect of smoke on the brain, during certain speeches.
There was some reference to the habit of cigarette-smoking in Canadian children. Unfortunately, many of them begin smoking when they are very young. Among their more active members are those in their early teens.
A survey conducted in Canada shows that one half of the boys and one third of the girls are habitual smokers at age 17. If one refers to a survey conducted by a James B. Morrison and published in the Canadian Journal of Public Health in 1964-in that case the survey was conducted among children between grades 5 and 12 in a Winnipeg school-one finds that children smoke very little before age 12, and that progress in school was slower among smokers and this, to a marked degree.
Tobacco addiction finds most of its recruits between the ages of 12 and 16 and, as I said before, at the age of 17, 50 per cent of the boys and 30 per cent of the girls declared themselves smokers. Of course, at the age of 18, those ratios have increased to 55 per cent and 33 per cent respectively.
Finally, let us say, that there is quite a close relationship between the smoking habit among students and their parents. According to the same inquiry, published in the Canadian Journal of Public Health, boys smoked more if one or the other of their parents or both smoked. This is also true of girls, but that habit was connected more frequently with that of the mother. That parental habit influences the girls more than the

boys, according to the studies which have been made.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Reports have also shown that the parents' example in this field will necessarily contribute to increase, decrease or abolish the smoking habit in young people and teenagers. In the United States, 68 per cent of men and 32 per cent of women of 18 years or more were registered among regular cigarette smokers.
Mr. Speaker, I simply wish to show that this bill seems absurd at first sight, especially on reading subsection 1 of clause 4:
-Every one is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction in the case of a first offence to be reprimanded, in the case of a second offence to a penalty not exceeding one dollar, and in the case of a third or subsequent offence to a penalty not exceeding four dollars, who, being under the age of IS years, smokes or chews-
And I doubt that one could chew at 13 years of age-
-tobacco in a street or public place, or purchases or has in his possession, whether for his own use or not, any cigarettes or cigarette papers, or purchases or has in his possession for his own use tobacco in any form other than cigarettes.
I hardly need to tell those who have reached a certain age and who have lived a bit, that children hide to smoke corn silk, particularly in the fall.
Contrary to my hon. colleague from York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), I feel that chapter 266 should be maintained as is in the statutes.
It is already a warning, and one representative of authority. And when the young people read or hear about someone who, 60 odd years before thought of them so that they might not be caught by the habit that will lead them to an early grave, I feel they will appreciate it. This may represent a very small benefit, but it is something that should stay in our mores since we are a people who have always had and continue to have a healthy fear of authority and who submit to it willingly, since fear is often the beginning of wisdom.
Section 4 of this act to restrain the use of tobacco among young people stipulates that a person guilty of a first offence is liable to be reprimanded and, in the case of a second offence, to a penalty of one dollar, as I have said. But this is symbolic rather than punitive. And I am sure that in certain areas today, the law is enforced not as a penal law but simply as a reprimand, to warn children that they are getting into a very dangerous habit.


Mr. Speaker, times have changed, but people have always remained relatively stable in their modus vivendi. As I said before, this act is enforced from time to time and appropriately so. And I cannot understand why it should be repealed, since it is now considered as part of prophylactic medicine, inspiring fear while at the same time pointing out a great danger: slow and painful death by lung cancer.
I hope that someday-resolutions to this effect have been brought forward in the house before-a skull will be printed on packages of cigarettes, under which there will be a warning of real danger, particularly for young people.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote-

speechtext:
-I should like to make a few remarks about this very interesting bill. This little bill concerns the Tobacco Restraints Act, and that act is not one I would want to see removed from our statutes. I do not say this because I disagree with the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) because I find myself in agreement with much of what he said. However, I should like to see this act remain on the statute books because it is a child's introduction to the statutes of Canada. I think it should be left there to continue to perform that purpose.
I can recall as a child, and I am sure other members of this chamber can, when it was a common thing to have the privilege of rushing down to the corner store on Sunday morning to get a package of cigarettes because there were none in the house. Generally there was some reward for this. In addition,
Tobacco Restraint Act one had a feeling of daring because he was violating a statute in performing the errand. I think it had a salutary effect.

subtopic: REPEAL OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING USE BY JUVENILES
speechtext: Had you read the statute then?

subtopic: REPEAL OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING USE BY JUVENILES

I had read it, and I read it at the age of six. It is for these reasons that I should like to keep it. I think this statute helps to stimulate wonderful addresses in the house, such as the address of the hon. member for York-Humber and hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather). The hon. member for New Westminster has a long and distinguished career in addressing the house on the subject of smoking. He was well known in British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, where he almost had a career as a non-smoker for years before coming to this house. As perhaps some hon. members know, he was the president of the Never-Touch-Em Club. He was not the founder of the Never-Touch-Em Club. That club was founded by a Vancouver newspaperman who thought of the idea of handing out badges which read, "Never-Touch-Em".
If you smoked you carried one of these badges behind the lapel of your coat, and when you gave up smoking you flashed the badge whenever people offered you a cigarette. This newspaperman had been president of the club and a non-smoker for some time. Then he was sent by his newspaper to do a story in South America and he was found skulking through the Andes with a fag in his lips. He had to relinquish the presidency of the Never-Touch-Em Club and the presidency then fell to the hon. member for New Westminster. He has upheld the tradition of that club without fail ever since. It is for this reason he is able to come before us and address the house on this subject, and it is for this reason we would like to hear him again. As I say, it is for this reason I do not want to see this statute removed from the statute books or we may be denied that privilege.
May I call it six o'clock?
